title: Don't ship a beautiful UI that doesn't help users finish the task
rule: A UI sets the tone within seconds; people stay or leave quickly. A polished visual layer (buttons, typography, graphics) is wasted if users struggle to complete basic tasks, get lost in navigation or can't find what they need. UI and UX are "two sides of the same coin"; you can't have one without the other.
why: Visual brilliance without usable flows goes to waste; the interface immediately sets the tone for the whole experience.
doDont: Bad example (thumbs-down): a flight-booking landing page ("Book your dream flight in just a few clicks!") with a gorgeous illustrated airplane hero, clean nav, but the only call to action is a single blue "Search flights" button. There is no way to enter From/To/Dates on the page, so the headline promise ("a few clicks") isn't supported by the UI (from visual).
auditCheck: Does the hero/landing promise a task (search, book, sign up) that the first screen lets the user start directly? Is the primary task reachable without extra navigation? Is there decorative imagery but no task-entry component?
restyleFix: Put the task's core input (e.g. search form) directly in the hero, keep the visual styling, and make the primary action live there.

title: Don't ship good UX with an unpolished, bare UI
rule: Even with rigorous research (personas, documented needs, mapped flows), neglecting UI quality yields a product that feels outdated or unpleasing and may lose to more visually appealing competitors.
why: A functional, user-centred product still "might not stand a chance against more visually appealing competition".
doDont: Bad example (thumbs-down): same flight page, now with the full search form (Return/One way, Economy class, 1 passenger, 2 luggages; From Vienna VIE → To London STN; Departure Friday 17 June; Return Sunday 19 June; Search) but styled raw: no imagery, flat grey page, black square-cornered outline box and black rectangular "Search" and "Sign up" buttons, plain text, no icons, no elevation, small headline (from visual).
auditCheck: Is the form functional but visually flat – default black/grey buttons, hard 1px outlines, no brand colour, no depth, no iconography, no imagery?
restyleFix: Keep the flow, add visual polish: brand colour primary button with rounded corners, soft card elevation for the search panel, small accent icons for fields/dropdowns, supporting imagery.

title: Combine strong UX and strong UI so the product is intuitive and loved
rule: The magic happens when both are right: a product that looks good and is intuitive/user-friendly. UI principles are not only about making things pretty but about giving people a good experience.
why: Good aesthetics + good flow => intuitive, user-friendly, loved.
doDont: Good example (thumbs-up): same flight page with the illustrated airplane hero on the right and the search form placed as a floating, rounded, soft-shadowed white card overlapping the hero image; blue filled "Search" button (primary), small amber/orange accent icons on the passenger/luggage dropdowns, arrows between fields and radio dots; light-blue tinted top row for trip options; light-blue "Sign up" button in nav; active nav item has a dot (from visual).
auditCheck: Does the hero combine imagery + the task component? Is there one clear primary button, a card elevation separating the form from the background, and consistent accent colours/icons?
restyleFix: Elevate the form into a card (rounded corners, soft shadow), colour the primary CTA, add subtle accent icons to fields.

title: Know the 15 core UI principles the playbook is built on
rule: The playbook's foundation principles are: Visual hierarchy, Proximity, Clarity, Alignment, Contrast, Simplicity, Whitespace, Layout, Balance & harmony, Consistency, Visual cues, Depth and texture, Color theory, Typography, Interaction cost. They underpin the practical tips and "elevate designs from good to exceptional".
why: Principles are the foundation; the book shows real-world examples to implement them and avoid pitfalls.
doDont: Grid of 15 icon tiles (4 columns x 4 rows, last row has 3) listing the principles; no good/bad pair.
auditCheck: Use as the checklist taxonomy: tag every finding with one of the 15 principles.
restyleFix: n/a (organising taxonomy).

title: Express importance through size, colour, weight and position
rule: Visual hierarchy = arranging elements to show relative importance and guide the eye, attention and actions, using size, colour, weight and position. If everything has the same size and colour, nothing stands out.
why: "You're basically shouting all the information at once, and nobody knows what to focus on."
doDont: Don't: shopping cart (Avocado $4.50, Lime $4.20, Orange $2.50, Total $11.20) where every button – three "Remove" buttons, "Continue shopping" and "Checkout" – is the identical dark-navy/purple filled rectangle, so all look equally important (thumbs-down).
auditCheck: Count filled/solid buttons with identical colour+size per decision group AND per viewport (the global header/nav is part of the first viewport, sticky or not; inference). More than one equal-weight primary-styled button in either, the same CTA (label + destination) filled twice in one viewport, or destructive row-level actions styled like primary CTAs = violation.
restyleFix: Assign one primary, one secondary, one tertiary style (see A-07/A-08) and demote repeated row actions.

title: Colour-coding buttons alone doesn't create hierarchy
rule: Giving each button a different colour (red "Remove", blue "Continue shopping", green "Checkout") but keeping the same size and style still leaves users unsure which action matters most.
why: Colour differentiates but doesn't rank; all buttons keep equal visual weight.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, left): three red/pink filled "Remove" buttons (one per row), blue full-width "Continue shopping", green full-width "Checkout" – same size, same filled style, three competing colours.
auditCheck: Are multiple buttons different hues but the same fill/size/shape? Does a rainbow of solid button colours appear in one component?
restyleFix: Reduce to one saturated filled CTA; use neutral/ghost styles for the others (see A-07).

title: Make one primary action vibrant, secondary muted, tertiary text-only
rule: "Checkout" = primary: vibrant green filled button, easy to spot. "Continue shopping" = secondary: same size as Checkout but grey (light grey fill, dark text) so it demands less attention. "Remove" = least prominent: only red/pink coloured text with underline, no filled background.
why: Clear action ranking tells users what to do next.
doDont: Good (thumbs-up, right): green filled Checkout, light-grey filled Continue shopping (same size), small underlined pink/red "Remove" text link under each item. Rows keep price at right; unchanged layout otherwise.
auditCheck: Per action group: exactly one filled saturated button; secondary buttons use neutral/grey/outline; per-row destructive/repeated actions are text links (small, underlined or coloured text), not filled buttons.
restyleFix: Primary = brand-coloured solid; secondary = neutral grey fill (same size is fine); tertiary/destructive-in-row = underlined text link in red.

title: Don't let imagery overpower the key details
rule: Don't make decorative/supporting elements disproportionately large. In the cart, oversized product photos steal the spotlight from product name, price and quantity.
why: Upsets visual balance (principle covered later) and pulls the eye from important details.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, left): cart with very large round product thumbnails (≈ 70px in a ≈ 250px-wide card, from visual) dwarfing the text; name/price/remove small.
auditCheck: Is the image/thumbnail height larger than ~2-3x the line-height of the primary text block next to it, or does the thumbnail visually outweigh name+price? (threshold from visual, no numeric value given.)
restyleFix: Reduce thumbnail size (≈ 40px in the good variant, from visual) so text carries the row.

title: Don't emphasise secondary information (e.g. quantity) over primary information
rule: Even when balanced, if less critical info (quantity "1 piece") is shown in larger font and higher contrast than product name or price, hierarchy is wrong. Quantity is useful but must not draw attention from what the product is and what it costs.
why: Attention goes to the least important data.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, right): small thumbnails, product name (Avocado/Lime/Orange) rendered light grey and small, "1 piece" rendered larger and darker than the name, price at right normal.
auditCheck: Compare font-size/colour of item name, price, and meta (quantity, SKU, date): is meta size >= name size or meta colour darker than name colour?
restyleFix: Name = darkest/medium weight; price = clear; meta (quantity) = smaller + lighter grey.

title: Rank elements by user importance before designing
rule: Before touching the design, list all features/elements the UI must include and rank them by importance to the user; then use colour, size, position and contrast to highlight the key information and guide users.
why: Prevents emphasising the wrong elements ("a common mistake").
doDont: Process rule, no visual pair of its own.
auditCheck: For each screen, can you name the top 1-3 (inference) pieces of information/actions? Does the visual weight order match that ranking?
restyleFix: Make a ranked list; re-style so rank 1 gets the largest/darkest/most contrasted treatment, lower ranks recede.

title: In metric cards make the value bigger than the label
rule: In KPI/stat cards, the figures (e.g. $4,981.00, 591, 2,121, trend +3.2%) should be the most prominent text; the metric titles (Earnings, Sales, Views) should be small and secondary.
why: Users came for the numbers; large titles take focus away from the actual values.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, top row): dark cards with big bold titles "Earnings / Sales / Views" and tiny values ($4,981.00 with small green ↗3.2%, 591, 2121). Good (thumbs-up, bottom row): same dark cards with a small muted label above and a large bold value ("$4,981.00" with small green "↗ 3.2%", "591", "2,121" – thousands separator applied), sparkline at the bottom, small coloured icon dot top-right.
auditCheck: In stat/metric cards, font-size(value) > font-size(label)? Typical good ratio ≈ 2x+ (from visual). Are values formatted with thousand separators (2,121 vs 2121 in the bad version)?
restyleFix: Label: small (~12px), muted; value: large (~2x), bold, white/high-contrast; keep trend indicator small and coloured.

title: Darker/stronger text for the title, lighter for supporting text
rule: Darker colours draw more attention and signal importance; lighter colours recede. Title should be dark black, supporting paragraph grey – not the reverse.
why: A grey title with black body undermines the title's importance.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, left card): title "Personal Injury Law" in grey, paragraph ("Attorneys in this field handle cases related to accidents, injuries, and wrongful deaths, seeking compensation for victims") in dark black. Good (right card): title in near-black, paragraph in mid-grey. Both cards have two small round icons (scales, gavel) on top.
auditCheck: Compare contrast ratio/lightness of heading vs body in the same block: heading contrast must be ≥ body contrast (heading colour darker than body on light themes; lighter on dark themes).
restyleFix: Heading → text-primary (near-black); body → text-secondary (grey, still accessible).

title: Use a vibrant colour to highlight the key action
rule: Making a clickable element a vibrant colour (e.g. a blue button) contrasts with surrounding text and naturally guides the eye, reinforcing its importance.
why: Colour contrast with the rest of the content attracts attention.
doDont: Text-only guidance (no pair shown on this page).
auditCheck: Is the primary button/link the most saturated element in its region? Does it differ in hue/saturation from the neutral text around it?
restyleFix: Apply a saturated brand colour to the primary action only; keep other text neutral.

title: Differentiate information by size, weight, colour and icons instead of uniform label:value lists
rule: Don't present all information with equal styling (label: value rows). Use font weight, size, colour and visual cues like icons to direct attention to what matters (price, title, status, key specs, contact).
why: A uniform list gives no hierarchy, so users can't scan or spot key info.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, left): property card with house photo and then 8 identical rows: "Type: For sale", "Price: £1,273,279", "Location", "Size: 1634 sqft", "Bedrooms: 5", "Bathrooms: 3", then "Contact person: Jennifer Bloom", "Phone number" – same size, bold labels in left column + values in a second column. Good (thumbs-up, right): big bold price "£3,273,279" at top-left; "For sale" shown as a small pill/badge at top-right (soft yellow); title "Luxury 5-bed Villa" in bold below; grey address with a location pin icon; a row with three icon + value specs ("1634 sqft", "5 bed.", "3 bath." with bold numbers, light units) separated by thin dividers; a footer with a small avatar, name "Jennifer Bloom" in bold, and phone in grey. (Note price differs between versions in the PDF: £1,273,279 vs £3,273,279.)
auditCheck: Detail cards/pages that list ≥5 (inference) key:value pairs with identical font-size/weight/colour for every row; labels like "Price:" "Type:" repeated. Missing icons/badges for status, unformatted key metrics.
restyleFix: Promote price to the largest, bold; turn status into a badge; group specs into one icon+value row with dividers; drop labels where icon/format makes meaning obvious; reduce contact info to avatar + name + phone.

title: Group related items closely and separate unrelated ones (Law of Proximity)
rule: Elements close together are perceived as related; those far apart as separate (Gestalt Law of Proximity). Spacing between items must therefore encode grouping; equal spacing everywhere erases grouping.
why: Correct proximity significantly reduces cognitive load; equal gaps make users second-guess which label goes with which field.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, left form "Contact details"): the "Surname" label sits 28px below the "Name" field and 28px above its own "Surname" field – equal 28/28 spacing, ambiguous. Form fields: Name, Surname, Street address, City/Town, Occupation, Images (Browse).
auditCheck: For stacked label+input pairs, gap(label→its input) must be clearly smaller than gap(previous input→this label). Flag if the two gaps are equal or the ratio is < ~2:1 (inference) (the example is 12 vs 32 = ~2.7:1).
restyleFix: Reduce label→input gap and increase field-group gap (see A-16).

title: Use ~12px label-to-field and ~32px field-to-next-label spacing
rule: Example of correct application: "Surname" label 12px from its own field and 32px from the "Name" field above.
why: Closer = related; makes it crystal clear which label belongs to which field.
doDont: Good (thumbs-up, right): label–field gap 12px, gap to the previous field 32px (annotated with magenta 32 / 12 tags); fields are light-grey filled rounded inputs.
auditCheck: Form CSS: label margin-bottom ≈ 12px (or 8-12 (inference)), field-group margin-bottom ≈ 32px; i.e. inter-group gap ≥ ~2.5x intra-group gap (inference).
restyleFix: Set label margin-bottom 12px; set group gap (field → next label) 32px (Tailwind e.g. `mb-3` label, `space-y-8` between groups).

title: Clarity: make interaction understandable without confusion
rule: Clear interfaces let users understand how to interact without getting lost: straightforward navigation, intuitive layouts, easily readable text. A clear interface minimises time and mental effort. Three common mistakes undermine it: oversimplification, overwhelming complexity, misguided UX.
why: Lack of clarity makes tasks hard and elements' purposes unclear.
doDont: Intro; examples follow in A-18 to A-20.
auditCheck: Can a first-time user say what each control does and what happens next without guessing? Check the three failure modes below.
restyleFix: see A-18 to A-20.

title: Don't oversimplify: keep essential labels and context
rule: Over-simplified designs lack the context users need to know what to do next. Keep text labels with icons/toggles.
why: Simplicity taken too far backfires; users can't tell what each control does.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, left "Smart home settings"): three tiles each with only a coloured icon (shield, lamp, arrows) and an off-state toggle, no text. Good (thumbs-up, right): same three tiles with labels "Home security", "Lights", "Air conditioning" plus toggles shown in both states (green = on for Home security and Air conditioning, grey = off for Lights) and meaningful icons (shield, bulb, fan).
auditCheck: Icon-only controls (toggles, tiles, nav) with no visible label/aria-label/tooltip; toggles whose on/off state isn't visually distinguishable or labelled.
restyleFix: Add a visible text label under/next to each icon; use clear on/off colours (green on, grey off); choose self-explanatory icons.

title: Don't overwhelm: limit options, buttons and information
rule: Interfaces packed with excessive options, buttons and info increase cognitive load and make decisions and finding things harder, even if you think you're giving more control.
why: Over-complexity is as bad as over-simplification.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, left): dark mobile "Dashboard" with orange accents: hamburger, "16 Habits", "Get Premium" badge, gauge, three outlined stat boxes (Average Self Rating, Habits Active, Habits Completion), two big orange buttons (Add More Habits / Track Your Habits), "Recommended Habits" list with many orange "+" buttons (hydrate, Exercise, Sleep…, Get Outside), a 3-column category grid (Mood, Productivity, Health) with more "+" items, total score, weekly score bar, FAB "+" and bottom nav of 4 tabs (Routines, Track Habits, Dashboard, Rate Day); tiny text, outlines everywhere, single orange used for everything. Good (right): calendar week strip (December 2023, M–S with the selected day 18 highlighted in lime), one big ring "Burned calories 652 Cal", three small rings (Steps 6540, Time 45 min, Heart 72 bpm), "Finished workouts" list with check items, icon-only bottom nav with selected state; lime accent, lots of space.
auditCheck: Number of distinct interactive elements per screen (e.g. > ~7-10 competing actions, multiple stacked sections each with own CTA); duplicated accent colour on everything; small text. (No numeric threshold is given in the PDF.)
restyleFix: Cut to a focused set of key metrics/actions; use progressive disclosure; group via rings/cards; reserve accent colour for the active/selected state.

title: Don't mislead: make copy and control states say the same thing
rule: Even a balanced design fails clarity if the UX is incorrect or misleading: instructions and control states must agree.
why: Misleading UX makes users do the wrong action.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, left): list of Raspberries (checked), Mango, Pistachios (checked), Kiwi with title "Unselect items you want to remove" and green Save – the checked items would be the ones kept, which inverts the usual meaning and the checkbox semantic. Good (right): title "Select items you want to remove" with Mango and Kiwi checked, same Save button – checked = affected item, instruction matches the control behaviour.
auditCheck: Does the checkbox/toggle's checked state match the verb in the label/title (check = act on)? Do instructions use negated/inverse logic ("unselect to…")? Are default states pre-checked in a way that contradicts the instruction?
restyleFix: Rewrite the instruction to positive, direct form ("Select items you want to remove"); ensure checked = the thing that will happen; no default pre-checked contradiction.

title: Align elements on shared axes for order and polish
rule: Alignment = arranging text, images and components along common lines/axes to create visual order and harmony. Poor alignment looks messy and is hard to use.
why: Gives a polished, organised look; misalignment hurts readability and perceived quality.
doDont: Intro to the following two examples (A-22, A-23).
auditCheck: Do left edges of titles, body text, buttons, icons within a component fall on the same x line (unless intentional hanging icon)? Check computed left offsets/padding.
restyleFix: Snap all items to common axes (see A-22 - A-28).

title: Don't misjudge alignment: icon, title, body and button should share a clean edge
rule: Alignment can be wrong by misjudgement: aligning things incorrectly (e.g. text indented next to an icon so the body and button no longer line up with the title).
why: Incorrect alignment creates a ragged, messy card.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, left card "Cactus"): title "Cactus" at left edge; below it a round cactus icon at the left edge with paragraph and "Learn more" pill button indented to the right of the icon, so the body/button don't align with the title. Good (right card): icon and title in one row at the top; paragraph and "Learn more" button below, both flush left on the same left edge as the icon.
auditCheck: In cards, does body/button left edge equal title/icon left edge? Is an icon floated alongside a multi-line paragraph, causing text indentation?
restyleFix: Put icon + title in a header row; place body text and button below on the card's common left edge.

title: Don't forget to align items: list items must share left/right edges
rule: Bad alignment also happens when you forget to align things properly; list items need identical edges.
why: Staggered edges look sloppy.
doDont: Bad (thumbs-down, dark "Resources" list with dashed guideline overlay): pill items "All", "Illustrations", "UI resources", "Icons" have different left/right edges and different offsets of icon and label (staggered by a few px, from visual). Good (right): all four pills share the same left and right edges, icons share an x-axis, labels share an x-axis.
auditCheck: Menu/list items: identical `x` and `width`, same icon column x, same label x. Compare bounding boxes in Figma/DOM.
restyleFix: Use one container with consistent padding and `flex-col` with `align-items: stretch`; same icon size & gap.

title: Left-align most text, especially long text and lists
rule: Left alignment is the go-to for most text; it creates a clean left edge that's easy to read, especially for paragraphs and lists.
why: Clean, consistent starting edge speeds reading.
doDont: Text guidance only.
auditCheck: Paragraphs/lists with `text-align: center` or right (in LTR).
restyleFix: Set `text-align: left` (`text-left`) for body text and lists.

title: Right-align numbers (and RTL languages)
rule: Right alignment suits numbers such as prices or table data because values line up from the right, making comparisons at a glance easier. It's also the correct alignment for RTL languages like Arabic.
why: Easier value comparison.
doDont: Text guidance only.
auditCheck: Numeric table columns left-aligned or centred; decimals/digits not lining up; use of `tabular-nums`? (the latter not mentioned; only right alignment).
restyleFix: `text-align: right` (`text-right`) on numeric columns (and their headers); RTL pages use right alignment.

title: Centre-align only short, standout items (titles, CTAs), never long text
rule: Centre alignment works for things that need to stand out, like titles or call-to-action buttons; avoid it for longer text blocks.
why: Starting point of each line changes, so eyes work harder to track the text.
doDont: Text guidance only.
auditCheck: Centre-aligned paragraphs with more than ~1-2 lines (threshold not specified in PDF).
restyleFix: Switch multi-line centred copy to left alignment; keep centring for headings and button labels.

title: Use a layout grid to align elements consistently
rule: Implement a grid system to make aligning easier and keep consistency across different parts of the UI.
why: Grids give shared columns and gutters.
doDont: Example: Figma "Layout grid" overlay (pink FF17BE at 17% opacity columns) behind three cards ("Alignment", "Visual hierarchy", "Proximity"), each card sitting exactly in one column. Settings: Columns, Count: 3, Colour: FF17BE 17%, Type: Stretch, Width: Auto, Margin: 79, Gutter: 70.
auditCheck: Do element widths/left edges match a column+gutter grid? Are margins/gutters consistent across sections? Check for a defined container/grid (CSS grid, Tailwind `grid-cols-*`, Figma layout grid).
restyleFix: Define a column grid (count, margin, gutter) and snap components to columns.

title: Use auto-layout so elements stay placed correctly
rule: Auto-layout ensures every element sits exactly where it should without manual nudging.
why: Avoids manual alignment errors.
doDont: Text guidance only.
auditCheck: Are positions set by absolute offsets/manual nudges (absolute positioning, manual margin hacks) instead of flex/grid/auto-layout and consistent gap?
restyleFix: Rebuild with Figma auto-layout / CSS flex/grid with consistent padding and gap tokens.

title: Pick one alignment strategy and apply it consistently across similar elements
rule: Choose an alignment strategy (e.g. everything left-aligned) and stick with it across similar elements so the design feels cohesive. Do not mix left and centre alignment inside the same component.
why: Consistent alignment creates a cohesive feel; mixing strategies looks accidental.
doDont: Dark-mode product card, same content in both. **Don't** (thumbs-down, labelled "Alignment: Left & Center"): the rating line and the author/brand line are centred while image edge, title and the price/"Add to basket" row are left-aligned, so the dashed alignment guides don't line up. **Do** (thumbs-up, labelled "Alignment: Left"): image, rating, title, author, price and button row all share the same left edge (dashed left guide runs straight down). (from visual) The top of the page also shows a Figma Auto-layout panel on a "Task progress" card (Copywriting 3/8, Illustrations 6/10, UI design 2/7 with coloured progress bars): vertical direction, gap **24**, horizontal padding **32**, vertical padding **32** – i.e. auto-layout is a way to keep spacing/alignment consistent (from visual; the page text does not explain it).
auditCheck: Within one card/section, do text blocks use more than one `text-align` (left + center) or different x-origins for siblings? Look for `text-center` on some children and `text-left` on others in the same container; flag mixed alignment among similar elements.
restyleFix: Pick one alignment (default left for text-heavy UI) and apply it to every sibling in the component; remove stray `text-align:center`/`items-center` on individual children. Use auto-layout/flex with fixed gap and padding tokens (example from visual: gap 24, padding 32).

title: Use contrast for readability, guidance and accessibility
rule: Contrast is what makes different things on screen stand out from each other so the important ones are easy to see. It serves three goals: (1) Readability – text and images easy to read; (2) Guidance – directs user focus and encourages interaction with specific elements; (3) Accessibility – content visible to users with visual impairments, meeting standards like WCAG.
why: As listed above (readability, guidance, accessibility/WCAG compliance).
doDont: n/a (principle; the example is in B-03).
auditCheck: Does every text/background pair and every key interactive element (primary CTA, active state) stand out clearly from its surroundings? Run a contrast-ratio check on all text, labels, badges and icons.
restyleFix: Raise contrast on low-contrast text/controls; reserve the strongest contrast for the most important element on screen.

title: Check contrast ratios on coloured status badges / chips (use darker text on a tint instead of white-ish text on a saturated fill)
rule: Badge/pill text must meet accessible contrast. The PDF shows measured ratios: bad badges **2.84:1, 1.81:1, 1.92:1**; good badges **4.8:1, 4.94:1, 6.54:1**. (The PDF names WCAG but does not state the threshold; the standard WCAG AA minimum for normal text is 4.5:1 – external knowledge, consistent with all "good" ratios being ≥4.8.)
why: Low-ratio badges are hard to read and fail accessibility standards.
doDont: Row of three ticket cards ("Ticket 122 – Brainstorm ideas for a feature – Blocked", "Ticket 231 – Wireframes for the new UI – In progress", "Ticket 431 – Analyze user feedback – Blocked"). **Don't**: badges are saturated fills (red/pink "Blocked", orange "In progress", bright green "Blocked") with white text → ratios 2.84, 1.81, 1.92. **Do**: badges use a pale tinted background (light pink, light peach, light green) with a dark, same-hue text colour → ratios 4.8, 4.94, 6.54. (colours from visual)
auditCheck: Compute contrast ratio of badge/tag/chip text against its fill; flag < 4.5:1 (ratios in the PDF's bad example are 1.81–2.84). Look for white text on bright mid-tone fills (e.g. bright green #22c55e-like, orange, light red).
restyleFix: Switch to the tint pattern: light tint background (e.g. `*-100`) + dark text of the same hue (e.g. `*-700/800`), then re-measure until ≥ 4.5:1.

title: Create contrast with colour (complementary / analogous hues) while respecting accessibility
rule: Use complementary or analogous colours to differentiate elements; keep accessibility guidelines in mind so contrast is good.
why: Colour difference separates elements and guides attention.
doDont: Text only (no dedicated visual beyond B-03).
auditCheck: Are adjacent distinct elements (e.g. primary vs secondary action, active vs inactive tab) distinguishable by hue/lightness, and does each colour pair pass contrast checks?
restyleFix: Pick differentiating colours from a deliberate palette (complementary/analogous) and verify ratios.

title: Create contrast with font weight and style
rule: Vary font weights and styles to create contrast within textual elements (e.g. bold title vs regular body).
why: Differentiates text roles without needing more colour/size.
doDont: Text only.
auditCheck: Do headings/labels/values differ in weight from body text? Flag screens where all text uses a single weight (e.g. everything `font-normal` or everything `font-semibold`).
restyleFix: Assign weights by role (e.g. titles/values 600–700, body/meta 400) consistently.

title: Create contrast with size
rule: Use size contrast to differentiate between elements; this sets up a clear visual hierarchy.
why: Size difference signals importance.
doDont: Text only.
auditCheck: Is there a visible size step between the primary element (title, key metric, CTA) and secondary elements? Flag type scales where adjacent levels differ by almost nothing.
restyleFix: Increase the size of the most important element and/or reduce secondary text so the hierarchy is clear.

title: Use a border or outline when elements are too similar in colour
rule: If elements are too close in colour (e.g. card on same-colour background, input on same-colour surface), add a well-placed border/outline to supply the missing contrast.
why: Border adds separation when colour difference is insufficient.
doDont: Text only.
auditCheck: Compare fill of component vs its parent background; if nearly identical and no border/shadow, flag (e.g. white input on white card without border).
restyleFix: Add a 1px subtle border (neutral tint) or outline to the element.

title: Use shadows to make an element pop from its background
rule: A shadow can make an element pop from its background, improve its visibility and create a sense of dimension.
why: Visibility and depth.
doDont: Text only (the panda cards in B-09 and cards throughout the pages show soft, diffuse shadows under raised cards – from visual).
auditCheck: Do raised/floating elements (cards, dropdowns, modals) separate from their background through a shadow or border? Flag floating layers with neither.
restyleFix: Add a soft, diffuse shadow to raised surfaces (keep it subtle).

title: Keep text over images legible for any image: add an overlay/gradient or a background blur
rule: For components with text over a background image, design for legibility at scale: light text on a dark photo may look fine, but it may fail when a lighter image is used. Make the component robust to any background by placing an overlay (with a layer blur that complements the image tone) or by using a background blur behind the text.
why: Content/images vary; legibility must not depend on one particular photo.
doDont: Three identical "Panda photography – By Aaron Burden" image cards. **Don't** (thumbs-down): title and small byline sit directly on the busy photo with no treatment – byline barely legible. **Do** (thumbs-up #1): a dark gradient overlay fades up from the bottom of the image behind the text. **Do** (thumbs-up #2): a blurred/translucent darkened panel (background blur) sits behind the text block at the bottom of the card. (from visual)
auditCheck: Is text positioned directly over a photo/video with no scrim, gradient, or `backdrop-filter: blur()`? Test with a light image; flag if contrast of text vs worst-case background < 4.5:1 (inference: WCAG AA threshold is not stated on p.22).
restyleFix: Add a bottom-to-top dark gradient scrim (or `backdrop-blur` + semi-transparent dark layer) behind the text; or move text to a solid panel.

title: Reduce elements and content to their essentials
rule: Simplicity = reducing elements and content to their most essential forms; prioritise essential features and information so users can accomplish their goals straightforwardly.
why: A simple design reduces cognitive effort and makes the interface easier to understand and navigate. Overcomplicated or cluttered designs overwhelm users, causing confusion and reduced engagement.
doDont: See B-11 (cart example).
auditCheck: For each screen, can the primary task be identified in a few seconds? Count competing elements/text lines per item; flag any element that doesn't support the screen's task.
restyleFix: Remove, collapse or defer non-essential elements; keep one clear primary action.

title: Cart screen: keep items compact, show only task-relevant details, and let whitespace/weight/colour do the work
rule: On a cart screen show only what's needed to check out. Size the product image appropriately so it doesn't fight other elements; use whitespace, font weights and font colours to organise info.
why: User is there to check out, not read extra info; too much makes the screen confusing and hard to understand quickly. The simpler version lowers cognitive load.
doDont: Two mobile "Cart" screens (back arrow, title, trash icon; "Luxury grey suit", $699 with −/1/+ stepper; "Total (3 items): $1797"; "Proceed to checkout" black pill; bottom nav with 4 icons). **Don't**: big product photos; many dark/bold detail lines per item (Color: Grey, Size: Medium (M), Material: Polyester, Viewed: 3221 times, Sold: 221 times, "* Read return policy"); items tightly packed so only ~2 items fit; total set very large/bold. **Do**: smaller product image; only Color and Size shown in light grey small text under a bolder product name; price + quantity stepper on one line; generous vertical gaps between items so 3 items visible; total in modest size. (from visual)
auditCheck: In cart/checkout lists, count metadata lines per line-item (PDF good example: name + 2 attributes + price/qty). Flag extra marketing/social-proof data (views, sold counts), return-policy notes, oversized images that push content/total below the fold.
restyleFix: Delete non-task metadata (viewed/sold counts, material, return notes → link elsewhere), shrink the thumbnail, set secondary attributes in lighter grey and smaller size, add spacing between items.

title: Show only information relevant to the user's current task
rule: Keep only the most important elements and information. Every additional button, image or line of text clutters the UI. Don't show users information that isn't relevant to the task they're trying to accomplish.
why: Cuts cognitive load and keeps focus where it should be.
doDont: Text only (see B-11).
auditCheck: For each element ask "does this help complete the task on this screen?" Flag buttons/images/text lines that don't.
restyleFix: Remove or move the irrelevant element to a secondary screen / progressive disclosure.

title: Give elements room to breathe with whitespace
rule: Whitespace ("negative space") is the unmarked area between design elements; it need not be white – any colour, texture or background image free of other elements counts. It gives room to breathe, enhances readability, guides focus and breaks up a page. Lack of whitespace makes an interface feel cramped and confusing.
why: Even when fonts, positions and colours are identical, whitespace alone can make or break the design.
doDont: Two "Tasking" app sidebars with identical fonts/positions/colours (Dashboard [active, tinted pill]; ANALYTICS: Performance, Mixpanel; SUPPORT: Tickets, Agents, Customers; SHOP: Products, Orders, Reports). **Don't**: items packed tightly, small padding around the active pill, tight gaps around section labels and dividers, so the list fits in less height. **Do**: more padding around logo, active pill larger with more inner padding, larger row height, and clear space around section labels/dividers; the whole list is taller, so fewer items are visible in the frame. (from visual)
auditCheck: Measure gaps between rows/groups: are list-item heights and group gaps clearly distinct, or do sections run together? Flag nav/list rows with vertical padding that is visually tight and group dividers with ~no margin.
restyleFix: Increase row height/padding and add larger gaps between groups than within groups.

title: Start with too much space, then scale down
rule: Start with more whitespace than you think you need, then reduce gradually until the balance is right.
why: Generous space gives flexibility to scale down. Starting with too little means you may not notice the clutter, resulting in a design hard to look at and navigate. (Over-generous space also isn't the final answer – it's a starting point.)
doDont: "Customer growth" card (line chart with "Total customers 179" tooltip, bars: Canada 88%, Greece 67%, France 43%, Pakistan 28%, "See more" button). p.26 shows two thumbs-down states: a loose version (large gaps between chart and rows, between rows, and before the button) and a cramped version (chart, rows, and button squeezed together, tooltip overlapping the title area). p.27 shows loose = thumbs-down, **balanced** version (moderate gaps – tighter than loose, clearly more than cramped) = thumbs-up. (from visual)
auditCheck: Are there crowded groupings (rows < ~8px apart (inference), chart tooltip colliding with title, button touching content)? Also flag the opposite: huge gaps that disconnect related items.
restyleFix: Increase spacing first to a generous level, then step down along the spacing scale until groups are clear but related items still read as related.

title: Establish a spacing and sizing system on a base unit
rule: Choose a base unit and work in multiples of it. Example: multiples of 4 → 4px, 8px, 16px, 24px, 32px, and so on. Systems based on multiples of 2, 4 or 6 are fine.
why: A standardised system gives consistent look and feel, speeds up design adjustments while keeping everything proportional, and reduces cognitive load because users' eyes/brain don't have to adjust to new spacing rules.
doDont: Contact form "Let's level up together" (subtitle "You can reach us anytime via hello@uxpeak.com", fields First name / Email / Message, checkbox "You agree to our friendly privacy policy.", "Send message" button). **Do** (thumbs-up): measured gaps annotated **16, 40, 8, 24, 24, 24, 40** (title→subtitle 16; subtitle→first field 40; label→input 8; between fields 24; between message and checkbox 24; checkbox→button 40) – all multiples of 8/4, with the same value reused for the same relationship. **Don't**: gaps **7, 19, 8, 19, 19, 21, 19** – arbitrary values with inconsistent relationships. (from visual; PDF text lists 16, 40, 40, 8, 24, 24, 24 and 7, 19, 19, 19, 19, 8, 21)
auditCheck: Extract all margin/padding/gap values; flag any not on the chosen grid (e.g. not multiples of 4). In Tailwind, flag arbitrary values like `p-[19px]`, `mt-[7px]`; in Figma flag spacing not from tokens.
restyleFix: Snap all spacing to the nearest scale step (4/8/16/24/32/40…); define spacing tokens; reuse one value per relationship type.

title: Tie the spacing system to the Law of Proximity (fixed value for related items)
rule: With a multiples-of-4 system, fix a rule such as "related items are 8px apart" and apply it throughout; larger steps separate unrelated groups.
why: Easy to apply consistently; simplifies cognitive load; aligns with Law of Proximity.
doDont: See B-15 (label→input always 8; fields apart 24; sections apart 40).
auditCheck: Is the gap within a group (e.g. label→input) always smaller than the gap between groups, and is the same value used everywhere for the same relationship?
restyleFix: Define tokens: e.g. intra-group 8px, between-field 24px, between-section 40px (values from visual of the form) and apply consistently.

title: Avoid random, non-multiplicative spacing numbers
rule: Don't use arbitrary spacing such as 31px or 19px.
why: Odd non-multiplicative numbers throw off harmony, disrupt rhythm, make the interface feel disjointed, and are harder to remember and reapply consistently.
doDont: Bad form from B-15 uses 7, 19, 21 etc.
auditCheck: Search CSS/Tailwind/Figma for spacing values like 7, 19, 21, 31px (not divisible by the base unit 4).
restyleFix: Round to the nearest scale value (e.g. 19→16 or 20/24, 31→32, 7→8).

title: Treat layout as both aesthetics and usability
rule: Layout is about not just what elements are on screen but where and how they're placed; it's the framework bringing aesthetics and usability together. Good layout (1) is visually pleasing, catching the eye and setting up a positive experience; (2) is intuitive, guiding the user logically through tasks so they find what they need.
why: As stated.
doDont: See B-19.
auditCheck: Does the visual flow (top→bottom / left→right) match the task order? Can users locate key info on first scan?
restyleFix: Re-arrange blocks into a logical reading order with clear grouping.

title: Prefer a simple single-column layout with a large hero image and generous whitespace over a cramped horizontal row separated by lines
rule: When showcasing a product/food item, use a simple single-column layout with a large eye-catching image and generous whitespace instead of cramming image, price and button in one small row separated by divider lines.
why: Visual appeal drives restaurant/food decisions ("we eat with our eyes"); a large appealing image makes the food look more premium and gives the perception of greater value. The streamlined design lets users scan multiple options quickly without getting bogged down in details.
doDont: Pizza card ("Italian pizza with tomato and salami", "$12 / 1 pizza", "Order now", description "Our authentic Italian pizza is made with the freshest ingredients and cooked to perfection."). **Don't**: wide card where the name is the most prominent element on top, then a row with small pizza thumbnail | price | orange Order-now button divided by vertical lines, with horizontal rules, and description in small text at the bottom. **Do**: narrow card with large pizza image on top, centred name, small grey description, price, full-width orange Order-now button, with generous padding. (from visual)
auditCheck: Are product cards using tiny thumbnails (when imagery is the main decision driver) and multi-column rows split by divider lines? Is the image the dominant element in visually-driven categories (food, travel, fashion, real estate)?
restyleFix: Convert to a single-column card: large image on top, then title, description, price, CTA; remove divider lines and rely on spacing.

title: Know what matters most to the user and make that element visually dominant
rule: Understand what's important to the user in the context (for restaurants: appealing imagery) and let layout prominence follow that, instead of giving prominence to e.g. the name.
why: Layout should reflect user priorities; image drives the decision in food contexts.
doDont: Same as B-19 (bad version gives prominence to the title; good version gives it to the image).
auditCheck: What is the largest/most prominent element on the card? Does it match the main decision driver for this domain?
restyleFix: Enlarge the decision-driving content (image) and demote secondary text.

title: Order elements in the sequence the user processes them: image → name → description → price → CTA
rule: With identical elements (same size and colour, large image), arrangement still matters. Good order: picture at top, then name, brief description, price, then the "Order now" button.
why: Order makes a noticeable difference to how the card reads; the CTA comes after the user has seen what the product is, what it is, and what it costs. (rationale is partly inferred; PDF only states that arrangement "makes a noticeable difference")
doDont: **Don't**: price at the top (above the image), then picture, name, Order-now button, and description last (below the button). **Do**: picture, name, description, price, Order-now button last.
auditCheck: Is the primary CTA last in the card flow, after identifying and price info? Is price floated above the image/title or description placed after the CTA? Flag CTA before descriptive content.
restyleFix: Reorder DOM/layout: media → title → description → price → CTA.

title: Turn plain radio-list options into selectable cards
rule: Replace a bland vertical list of text-only options with selectable cards. Each card can carry labels, colours, even icons or images for context and richness.
why: Plain lists give limited visual differentiation and aren't memorable; cards add interaction and visual appeal and make info more digestible and the interface more engaging.
doDont: Plan picker. **Don't**: single white box with three radio rows in one line of text each: "Basic - 10 credits (£5/month)", "Economy - 50 credits (£10/month)" [selected], "Pro - 100 credits (£15/month)". **Do**: three side-by-side cards – each with a coloured plan label pill (Basic / Economy / Pro; Economy in green), a radio at top-right, large bold number of credits ("10 credits", "50 credits", "100 credits") and price ("$5 / month", "$10 / month", "$15 / month"). Selected (Economy) card is larger/raised with a green border and filled radio. (from visual)
auditCheck: Are 2–5 (inference) plan/option choices rendered as plain text radio rows where each option has structured data (name, quantity, price)? Is the selected state visually obvious?
restyleFix: Make each option a card with label chip, key figure emphasised (big number), price secondary, a radio/check indicator, and a distinct selected state (border colour + scale/elevation).

title: Design form layout after the final output
rule: Take cues from how the submitted information will be displayed or used: structure and order the form fields/groups to mirror the final output.
why: Forms are critical touchpoints that are often dull; aligning them with the final result makes the process more interesting, intuitive and aligned with the user's goals.
doDont: "Final display" shows a classified-listing card: Image on top; "Toyota Rav4 Hybrid" + "$32,034" (Product & Price); description ("A 2023 Toyota RAV4 Hybrid, an eco-friendly, sleek SUV…") with "Posted 1 day ago"; Location row "Manchester, UK" with "View map" link; Tags/Categories chips (Hybrid car, Toyota, SUV). Labels with arrows map each region (Image, Product & Price, Description, Location, Tags/Categories) – i.e. the form should have those sections in that order/shape. The corresponding form is on the next page (outside this range).
auditCheck: Does the order and grouping of form fields match how the data will be shown (e.g. image upload first, title+price together, description, location, tags)? Flag forms whose structure is arbitrary relative to the output.
restyleFix: Reorder/group fields to mirror the final card; place related fields side by side as they appear in the output (e.g. name and price on one row).

title: Lay out creation forms to mirror the final result
rule: When users create content that will be displayed later (e.g. a marketplace listing), do not default to a standard linear stack of labelled fields. Arrange the form fields the way the information will appear on the final page (e.g. image area on top, item name and price side by side, then description, location, tag chip).
why: Gives users a sense of how the listing will look and function, making form-filling more relatable and engaging.
doDont: Don't (thumbs-down): a plain white card titled "Create new listing" with a vertical list of label + empty input pairs (Item, Price, Description, Categories, Location, Images with a "Browse" button). Do (thumbs-up, from visual): a card that looks like the finished listing, with a large grey image placeholder ("Add an image") at top, "Item" ("What are you selling?") and "Price" ("$0") in one row separated by a divider, then "Description" ("Describe what you're selling in more detail ..."), "Location" ("Enter your address"), and an "Add tag +" pill at the bottom. Fields are inline-placeholder style, separated by thin dividers.
auditCheck: Is a "create/list/post" form a generic linear label-over-input stack even though a known output layout (listing, profile, card, post) exists? Does field order/grouping differ from the order in which the data is shown on the result page?
restyleFix: Rebuild the form as an editable preview of the output: image slot at the top, title/price in one row, description below, location, tags; use placeholder text as labels where appropriate and thin dividers instead of boxed inputs.

title: Keep proportion and scale balanced – no element overpowers the others
rule: No single element should overpower the others. Every element gets its own space and prominence, but not so much that it becomes a distraction.
why: Balance and harmony make everything on the page fit together, make the design look good, easier to use, and help people quickly understand what is on screen and how to use it.
doDont: See C-04/C-05 (kiwi card example, p.37). Oversized elements are the "don't".
auditCheck: Is any one element (hero image, CTA, heading) disproportionately large relative to the rest of the component so that the eye has no clear second stop? Compare sizes of image, heading, body and button within a card.
restyleFix: Scale down the dominant element until the heading, body and CTA each remain easy to see without any of them dominating.

title: Use colour harmony – don't overuse a single colour
rule: Overusing one colour makes a design feel monotonous or overwhelming. Use complementary or analogous colours to bring variation and emotional balance.
why: Variation creates emotional balance; a single colour everywhere is monotonous/overwhelming.
doDont: See C-06 (kiwi example).
auditCheck: Is one hue used for image background, CTA and small accents all at once? Is the palette limited to a single hue with no complementary/analogous partner?
restyleFix: Reserve the strong accent for the primary action; use a softer/neutral or analogous/complementary tint for backgrounds and decorative elements.

title: Keep consistent spacing, typography and element sizes between components
rule: Maintain consistent spacing, typography and element sizes to create a harmonious relationship among all UI components ("element relationships").
why: Consistent relationships make the components feel like one system.
doDont: No dedicated example; the kiwi pair (p.37) shows the refined version with heading, body, rating and button at modest, proportionate sizes.
auditCheck: Do similar components use different paddings, font sizes or element heights? Are spacing/type/size values drawn from a shared scale/tokens?
restyleFix: Normalise spacing, type sizes and element sizes to a shared token scale across components.

title: Don't let the hero image and CTA button hog the card
rule: Image and button must not be too big compared to the rest of the content. Keep the image eye-catching but not overshadowing; make heading and CTA easy to see but "not too flashy".
why: When image and button are oversized, they hog attention; the eye doesn't know where to go next and crucial details (heading, description, rating) get lost.
doDont: Don't (from visual): kiwi-ice-cream card with a very large circle image, tiny description and rating text, and a full-card-width tall pill "Get now" button. Do (from visual): the image is smaller, the heading stays about the same size, the description and rating text are larger and more readable (the description grows relative to the heading), the rating row sits under it and the "Get now" button is a small, compact pill (not full width), the card is shorter.
auditCheck: Is the CTA full-width/very tall on a content card when it is not a mobile footer bar? Is the hero image taking the dominant share of card area while the description and rating text are tiny (compare description/rating size to the heading and the image)? Does the secondary content get visually lost?
restyleFix: Reduce image diameter/height, shrink CTA to content-width pill with normal padding, bump the description and rating text size (the heading can stay about the same) so the card reads heading → description → rating → CTA.

title: Don't paint everything the same colour (single-colour overuse)
rule: Don't use one colour (e.g. green) for the image background, the CTA and smaller elements simultaneously; distribute colours more evenly.
why: Overuse of a single colour makes the interface feel monotonous and a bit overwhelming.
doDont: Don't (from visual): saturated green circle behind the image, green decorative bits and a big green CTA. Do (from visual): image sits on a pale peach/cream circle with small pink/green confetti shapes; only the "Get now" button carries the green (lime) accent. Colours more even, not leaning on one hue.
auditCheck: Count surfaces/elements sharing the same saturated accent hue within one component; flag if the accent is on both a large background shape and the CTA (and other small items).
restyleFix: Replace large saturated backgrounds with a light neutral/complementary tint; keep the saturated accent for the CTA only.

title: Keep essential UI components consistent across the same and different screens
rule: Make elements function and look similar throughout the design – on the same screen and across screens. Consistency does not mean everything is identical (e.g. product pictures may have different backgrounds), but essential components – titles, buttons, input fields – must remain consistent.
why: (1) Ease of use – easier navigation; (2) Builds trust – looks more professional and reliable; (3) Reduces cognitive load – less mental effort; (4) Cohesive aesthetic – unified experience that resonates with users. Users learn the UI faster, improving usability and satisfaction.
doDont: Do vary content imagery (backgrounds of product pictures); don't vary the look/behaviour of titles, buttons, inputs.
auditCheck: Do the same component types (title, button, input) have different size, radius, colour, padding or behaviour on different screens/sections? Are there one-off component variants not in the design system?
restyleFix: Consolidate to a single component style per role (title, button, input) via shared tokens/components; allow variation only in content/imagery.

title: Use one corner-radius/shape language for all elements
rule: Use consistent corner radii across pictures, buttons and other elements; don't mix e.g. rounded pictures with square buttons.
why: Inconsistent radii confuse users, make the design look off-brand and fail to create a cohesive look. A consistent rounded appearance makes the UI easier to navigate and more pleasing (p.40 continuation).
doDont: Don't (from visual, three animal cards): lion picture is a circle but its "Book now" button is a square-cornered black rectangle; the hippo picture is a square image; the third card's avatars are square-ish and the middle card edge is square-cornered; others are rounded. Do (from visual): all three cards have circular images, pill-shaped black "Book now" buttons, rounded card corners and rounded avatars.
auditCheck: Collect all `border-radius` values (rounded-*, radius tokens) in a view; flag if sibling cards/buttons/images mix sharp (0) with rounded values or have more radii than the token scale (e.g. a button radius 0 next to rounded-full buttons).
restyleFix: Define radius tokens (e.g. card radius, button radius, media radius) and apply the same shape family (all rounded or all sharp) to cards, buttons, images, avatars.

title: Use one button colour scheme (primary/secondary/tertiary) everywhere
rule: Don't use many different colours for primary, secondary and tertiary buttons (e.g. tinted to match each card's image). Use one colour scheme for all buttons: black (dark) for main actions and light grey for secondary ones.
why: Different button colours make users wonder whether each button has a unique function, divert attention from main content and can feel off-brand. One scheme looks organised/professional and makes it obvious what each button does.
doDont: Don't (from visual): each of the three cards has its own button pair coloured to match the illustration (orange for lion, brown for hippo, purple for elephant; light tint "Learn more" + solid "Book now"). Do (from visual): all three cards use the same pair – light grey "Learn more" and near-black/dark brown "Book now".
auditCheck: Do equivalent buttons (same role) have different background colours across sibling cards/sections? Count distinct primary-button fills per screen (should be 1).
restyleFix: Define one primary and one secondary button style (dark fill / light-grey fill) and apply to every card regardless of illustration colour.

title: Normalise image shapes and sizes by placing them in a consistent container (e.g. circle)
rule: When images vary in shape and size, put them inside a consistent shape such as a circle, then adjust their size/positioning so they are the same size and in similar positions.
why: Varied shapes/sizes look out of place and disconnected with no unity or flow; the circle gives a cleaner, more put-together look.
doDont: Don't (from visual): three gift-box illustrations of different widths/heights floating on white, at slightly different vertical positions. Do (from visual): each gift box sits in a same-size circle with a soft tint (pale blue, pale pink, pale yellow), centred at the same spot above the title.
auditCheck: Do images/illustrations in a row of cards have different dimensions, aspect ratios or alignment? Is there a shared fixed-size mask/container (same width/height/radius)?
restyleFix: Wrap each image in a fixed-size circular (or other uniform) container with a subtle tint and centre the image; keep the same offset from the card top.

title: Make cards in a set (3+) the same height
rule: In a layout with three or more cards, all cards must have the same height.
why: Looks good and makes things easier and more straightforward for the user.
doDont: Don't (from visual): three accommodation cards (Forest Bungalows, Trailer Homes, Mountain Lodges in the Snowy Region of Scotland) of three different heights because the text lengths differ (short, shortest, longest) – ragged bottom edges and buttons at different y positions. Do: see C-12/C-13 (equal-height cards).
auditCheck: In a card grid/row of 3+, compare rendered heights and CTA y-offsets; flag if not equal (code: missing `align-items: stretch`/`h-full`/grid equal rows).
restyleFix: Use grid/flex stretch so cards share the tallest card's height (or fixed heights) and see C-13 for bottom-aligned CTAs.

title: Keep headings and descriptions about the same length across cards
rule: Make headings and descriptions about the same length so cards naturally share the same height; if you can influence UX copy, keep the same number of lines across all cards.
why: Keeps cards the same height and makes the design look more balanced.
doDont: Don't (p.43): card 3 title wraps to two lines ("Mountain Lodges in the Snowy Region of Scotland") with a long ~7-line paragraph, while the other titles are 1 line and their descriptions are 4 lines (Forest Bungalows) and 2 lines (Trailer Homes). Do (from visual p.44): titles shortened to "Forest Bungalows", "Trailer Homes", "Mountain Lodges"; each description is ~2 lines ("Surround yourself with the calming vibes of the forest in our cozy bungalows." / "Enjoy a nice stay in our comfy trailer homes. All the essentials without the big price tag." / "Stay in luxury among stunning mountains, where rustic charm meets modern comfort."); all cards equal height with buttons aligned.
auditCheck: Compare line counts of titles/descriptions among sibling cards; flag if they differ (e.g. more than a line difference (inference)) or text is much longer in one card.
restyleFix: Edit/trim copy so each title and description has the same line count (shorten the outlier); otherwise use C-13.

title: When copy length varies, equalise card height and pin CTAs to the bottom
rule: If you can't control UX copy and content varies, make all cards the same height but align the CTA buttons at the bottom of each card, leaving any extra space in the middle (between text and button).
why: Creates the illusion of uniformity even when content length varies.
doDont: Do (from visual p.44 bottom): three cards with different text lengths (Mountain Lodges long, Forest Bungalows medium, Trailer Homes medium), equal height, "Explore offers" buttons all on the same baseline at the bottom with empty space above the button in cards with shorter text. Don't: buttons directly under variable-length text at different heights (p.43 bad example).
auditCheck: In equal-height cards, are CTAs at identical y positions? (Code: card is flex column and CTA wrapper has `margin-top:auto`/`mt-auto`.) Flag CTAs that float at different heights.
restyleFix: Make the card `display:flex; flex-direction:column; height:100%` and push the button container with `margin-top:auto`.

title: Use a single icon style (outline vs filled, weight, detail, size) within a screen
rule: Don't mix icons of different sizes or types – e.g. one simple and another highly detailed, or some outlined and others filled on the same screen. Decide on an icon style ahead of time and use it across all UI screens (e.g. outlined everywhere).
why: Inconsistent icons are a common error that breaks cohesion.
doDont: Don't (from visual, "Account features" list): Manage account icon is a detailed double-person outline, search is a different outline, heart is filled, share is filled, notification bell is filled – mixed outline/filled and different detail levels, and icons slightly different sizes. Do (from visual): all five icons (user, search, heart, share, bell) are consistent thin outline icons of the same size and stroke, in the same purple colour.
auditCheck: Within a screen, do icons mix stroke and fill variants, different stroke widths, different sizes or different libraries? (Code: multiple icon packages imported, mix of `fill`/`stroke` styles, inconsistent width/height.)
restyleFix: Replace all icons with one set in a single style (e.g. outlined), same stroke width and the same size (grid).

title: Mix icon styles only to signal state (e.g. filled = selected tab)
rule: Exception: mixing icon styles is OK when it indicates different states. In bottom navigation, the selected tab uses a filled icon while the other tabs use outlined icons.
why: This subtle style change serves a functional purpose – helping users quickly identify their current location in the app.
doDont: Do (from visual p.46): dark bottom nav bar with four icons; the active "home" icon is filled, on a lilac circular highlight raised/notched in the bar; the other three (clock, pie chart, user) are outlined and grey; annotated "Icon: filled" and "Icon: outlined".
auditCheck: If a nav bar uses filled vs outline icons, does the difference map to selected/unselected state rather than arbitrary variation? Is the active tab differentiated (filled)?
restyleFix: In tab bars/nav, use outlined for inactive and the filled variant of the same icon for the active tab (optionally plus highlight).

title: Use one icon set (custom or open-source) that fits the brand
rule: A custom icon set is one way to achieve consistency, but open-source icons are fine if the set aligns with the overall brand image and you don't mix two different sets with varying properties.
why: Keeps a consistent look.
doDont: Do: one coherent set (custom or open-source) matching the brand. Don't: mix two different icon sets with different properties (weight, style, corner shape).
auditCheck: How many icon libraries are in the project/Figma file? Do icons across screens have different stroke weights, terminal shapes or corner styles?
restyleFix: Pick one library (e.g. a single open-source family matching brand tone) and swap out all others.

title: Add illustrations/progress indicators to make step content faster to grasp
rule: Use visual cues (illustrations, step indicators) rather than text-only presentation; they do more than add flair – they help users understand the message faster, make information easier to grasp, and make the interaction more engaging and memorable.
why: Visuals make learning and interaction more engaging and memorable and improve understanding speed.
doDont: Don't (from visual): three "Step 1/2/3" cards ("Place Your Order", "On the Way", "Get It Delivered") with only small grey "Step N" label, title and description text on white. Do (from visual): the same cards each with a themed illustration at top (person with phone/boxes, courier on bicycle, courier handing pizza at a door) and a 3-segment progress bar under it (green segment marks the current step: 1st, 2nd or 3rd of the three) above "Step N", title and description.
auditCheck: Are step/process/feature sections text-only with no iconography, illustration or progress indicator? Is there a visual representation of what each step means and where the user is in the sequence?
restyleFix: Add a relevant illustration/icon per step and a segmented progress indicator highlighting the step's position.

title: Represent senders with coloured initial avatars in lists (inbox/messaging)
rule: In email inbox/messaging lists, add a visual cue per sender: a coloured circular icon (from a set of colours) with the sender's first initial in the middle.
why: A plain text list, while functional, misses opportunities to enhance usability; avatars help scanning and distinguishing senders and make the UI creative and visually appealing.
doDont: Don't (from visual): list of rows (name, date right-aligned, bold subject, grey preview truncated with ellipsis) with no leading visual. Do (from visual): same rows with a leading circle containing a white initial letter – S (pink, Sarah Johnson), S (green, Starbucks), J (purple, John Doe), L (orange, Lyft); text is shifted right of the avatar, dates remain right-aligned.
auditCheck: Do list items (people/senders/contacts) lack avatars or leading visual identifiers? Are avatar colours distinguishable among different senders?
restyleFix: Add a circular avatar (~same height as two lines of text, from visual) with the first-letter initial in white on a per-sender colour; keep the text column aligned.

title: Represent senders with photos/logos, not plain text/initials
section: Sender representation in lists (continuation of previous chapter) (p.49)
rule: In message/inbox lists, represent each sender with an image: a photo for people, a logo for companies. Row layout shown (from visual): avatar at left, sender name bold with date right-aligned on the same line, subject line below, one-line truncated preview (grey, smaller, ellipsis) below that; rows separated by thin, light divider lines inset from the card edges; list sits in a white rounded card with soft shadow on a very pale background.
why: Users can easily identify the sender and quickly understand the context of the message.
doDont: Do (thumbs-up, the only example on this page): Sarah Johnson and John Doe with round photo avatars, Starbucks and Lyft with round brand logos. (The "don't" counterpart is on the previous page, outside this range.)
auditCheck: Does a list of people/companies (inbox, contacts, activity feed, comments) show only text or generic/placeholder icons when a photo or logo is available?
restyleFix: Add a ~32px circular avatar (photo or logo) at the leading edge of each row; fall back to initials only when no image exists.

title: Use depth and texture (shadows, outlines, background colour) to guide eyes and actions
rule: Treat depth and texture as core design principles. Create them through shadows, outlines or varying background colours so they guide where users look and what they do.
why: Beyond aesthetics they improve usability: they build visual hierarchy and make interactive elements more noticeable.
doDont: Do use depth cues to separate layers/sections and to flag interactive elements; don't leave an interface as one undifferentiated flat plane.
auditCheck: Can you tell, without reading, which elements are raised/interactive versus background? If every surface is the same colour with no shadow, outline or tone change, flag it.
restyleFix: Introduce a layering model: page background tone, surface (cards) tone, optional outline, and shadow tiers for floating elements (see D-08/D-09).

title: Give floating elements (dropdown menus) a subtle shadow
rule: Use shadows to create a sense of depth so users can tell which items they can click or move, and to move the design away from flat layouts. A navigation dropdown should have a subtle shadow so it appears to float above the page.
why: The shadow makes the dropdown seem to float above the page and helps the menu stand out from the background, making it easier to focus on the options.
doDont: Don't (left, thumbs-down): nav bar "Resources / Solutions / Pricing" with the open "Solutions" dropdown (Marketing, Product & Engineering, Customer experience, Customer engagement, footer "All resources") has no shadow, so the white panel merges with the pale grey background behind it. Do (right, thumbs-up): identical dropdown with a subtle, diffuse shadow that lifts it off the page.
auditCheck: Do dropdowns, popovers, menus, tooltips and modals have a box-shadow (or equivalent elevation) when overlapping other content? `box-shadow: none` on an absolutely/fixed-positioned overlay = violation.
restyleFix: Add a soft shadow to the overlay (see D-05 values, e.g. `0 12px 48px` low-opacity) so it separates from the underlying page.

title: Add shadows to elements overlapping dynamic/complex backgrounds
rule: When an element sits on top of a complex or variable background (e.g. a map), give it a shadow so it does not get lost. Example: the "Active users – Past week – 128,200" label over the US on a map, and the zoom +/- buttons at the bottom of the map.
why: Without shadows these elements risk blending into the complex, variable background.
doDont: Don't (left): map card where the 128,200 label chip and the +/- zoom buttons are flat white on the map, nearly blending in. Do (right): the same label chip and zoom buttons carry a soft shadow and visibly sit above the map.
auditCheck: Are labels, chips, controls or text containers placed over images/maps/video/charts without any shadow, border, or opaque contrast background?
restyleFix: Add a small soft shadow (sm tier, see D-09) to overlay chips and map controls.

title: Use soft, diffuse shadows – never harsh/tight dark ones
rule:
Shadows must be soft and blend with the background, adding just enough depth. Harsh or too-distinct shadows look overbearing and unprofessional. Reference values (Figma drop shadow, white card on very light grey page):
  - Bad: X 0, Y 0, Blur 48, colour #9F9F9F (strong, rough, dark grey halo all around the card).
  - Good: X 0, Y 12, Blur 48, colour #E9E9E9 (lighter, smoother, offset downward).
why: A common mistake is shadows too harsh/distinct; they create an overbearing effect and look unprofessional.
doDont: Don't: product card ("Only natural ingredients", lemon + dropper bottle image, yellow "Learn more" button) with a dark, wide, centred (Y 0) grey shadow. Do: same card with a very light grey shadow shifted down 12px (light comes from above) and the same 48 blur.
auditCheck: Is the shadow colour darker than ~#D0D0D0 equivalent (or alpha above roughly 10-15% black) (inference) on a light UI? Is Y offset 0 with large blur (halo all around)? Large blur (~48px) with light colour and positive Y offset (~12px) is the target pattern.
restyleFix: Replace with `box-shadow: 0 12px 48px <very light tint>` (e.g. #E9E9E9 on neutral bg), or lower alpha of existing shadow and add a positive Y offset.

title: Tint the shadow colour to match a coloured background
rule: Match shadow colour to the background hue instead of using neutral grey. Example on a light purple background: grey shadow (X 0, Y 19, Blur 48, #C7C7C7) vs purple-tinted shadow (X 0, Y 19, Blur 56, #CFC9DD).
why: Colour matters as much as softness/depth; grey looks like a safe bet but clashes with the purple background, breaking visual harmony and feeling jarring. A tinted shadow blends seamlessly and makes the design more cohesive.
doDont: Don't: "Be You, Only Better" card (woman with purple-lit image, yellow "Get flawless today" button) on pale purple page with a grey #C7C7C7 shadow. Do: same card with a purple-tinted #CFC9DD shadow and slightly larger blur (56 vs 48). Described as a "pro tip many junior designers don't know".
auditCheck: On any non-neutral page/section background, is the shadow colour a neutral grey/black (R=G=B) rather than a darker, low-saturation version of the background hue? Compare shadow hue with background hue.
restyleFix: Set shadow colour to a desaturated mid-tone of the background hue (e.g. #CFC9DD for a light purple surface) and keep it soft; optionally widen blur a few px.

title: Never use pure grey or black shadows on coloured backgrounds (yellow example)
rule: Once you know the tinting trick, don't use pure grey/black shadows on coloured backgrounds. Second worked example on a pale yellow/cream background: grey shadow (X 0, Y 20, Blur 60, #D8D8D8) vs warm-tinted shadow (X 0, Y 12, Blur 48, #E3D5B2).
why: Creates more coherent and engaging UIs; an easy but impactful improvement.
doDont: Don't: "Only natural ingredients" card (amber bottles-and-arch image, yellow "Learn more" button) on a cream background with neutral grey shadow, which looks dirty against the warm tone. Do: same card with a warm beige shadow (#E3D5B2) that sits naturally in the cream background.
auditCheck: Any shadow with equal R/G/B channels (grey/black, e.g. rgba(0,0,0,x)) over a tinted section background.
restyleFix: Swap neutral shadow for a warm/hue-matched tint (e.g. #E3D5B2 on cream) at similar softness; note the tinted version also used smaller Y (12 vs 20) and blur (48 vs 60).

title: Define a shadow system (named elevation scale) and use it consistently
rule: Create a shadow system: a rulebook of shadow styles applied the same way every time across all projects, matching your brand style (simple, flashy, or in between). Example scale shown has six named levels: xs, sm, md, lg, xl, 2xl.
why: Keeps the design consistent and in line with the brand, and improves user experience.
doDont: Visual shows six identical white squares on a pale grey panel with progressively larger/softer/lower shadows: xs = tight, crisp, almost outline-like; sm and md = small soft shadow beneath; lg = medium diffused; xl and 2xl = large, wide, strongly offset diffuse shadows (from visual; exact values not given).
auditCheck: Count distinct `box-shadow` values in the CSS/tokens. Ad-hoc, one-off values per component (many near-duplicates) = violation; expect a small defined set (e.g. xs/sm/md/lg/xl/2xl or at least 3 tiers (inference)) exposed as tokens.
restyleFix: Consolidate shadows into named tokens (e.g. `--shadow-xs … --shadow-2xl` / Tailwind `shadow-*`) with monotonic increase in Y offset and blur, then map each component to a token.

title: Have at least three shadow tiers mapped to element purpose
rule:
Start with at least three styles:
  1. Soft shadow – general elements you want to slightly lift off the page: buttons, small cards, thumbnails.
  2. Medium shadow – elements that need more focus: modals, pop-up windows. A bit darker and with more spread than soft.
  3. Strong shadow – elements that must really stand out / appear elevated: dropdown menus, important alerts.
why: Elevation should reflect importance/focus level of the element.
doDont: Do map tier to element role (small & static = soft; focus-demanding overlays = medium; highest, most prominent = strong). Don't use the same shadow for everything, or a heavier shadow on minor elements than on overlays.
auditCheck: Is a modal's shadow weaker than a small card's? Do buttons/thumbnails carry large, dark shadows? Is there a visible difference between button, modal and dropdown elevations?
restyleFix: Assign soft to buttons/small cards/thumbnails, medium to modals/popups, strong to dropdowns/important alerts; increase blur/spread/darkness with tier.

title: Create variations of shadow styles for specific needs
rule: Each shadow tier can have variants for specific needs, e.g. a medium shadow with a different colour tint for warning messages, or a really subtle shadow for text boxes.
why: Shadows should be adaptable to context while staying within the system.
doDont: Do derive variants (tinted, extra-subtle) from the base tiers; don't invent unrelated one-off shadows.
auditCheck: Do warning/alert components and inputs use a variant derived from the system (tinted or subtler), or an unrelated hard-coded shadow?
restyleFix: Add token variants such as `shadow-md-warning` (tinted) and `shadow-input` (very subtle).

title: Use background-colour layering (light grey page + white cards) instead of all-white
section: Depth through outlines and background colours (p.56-58)
rule: Create depth by subtly changing background colour to distinguish sections/elements. Pure white for page and elements can work but can look too plain. Use a light grey page background with white cards on top for a layered effect. Especially valuable in information-dense interfaces such as dashboards, but not limited to them.
why: Gives a more structured look and makes it easier for users to focus on specific sections.
doDont: Don't (top, thumbs-down): "Tasking" dashboard where main content area, sidebar, KPI stats (Sales $92,200 / Website visits 121,520), and Customer Growth chart are all on one flat white surface with no separation. Do (bottom, thumbs-up): content area has a light grey background, with Sales, Website visits and Customer Growth each in separate white cards; sidebar is white and divided from content by a thin vertical line (from visual).
auditCheck: Is the page background identical to card/panel surface colour (e.g. #FFFFFF on #FFFFFF) with no border or shadow separating regions? In dashboards, are widgets/sections floating on one white plane?
restyleFix: Set page/canvas background to a very light grey (e.g. ~#F5F5F7-ish, from visual; no value given) and keep cards/panels pure white.

title: Alternatively segment areas with thin outlines
section: Depth through outlines and background colours (p.56-58)
