rule: Outlines can create the same separation as background colour: use thin lines to segment areas, guide the eye and create natural divisions. Applied example (from visual): each widget (Sales, Website visits, Customer Growth) is in a card with a thin light outline; sidebar sections are divided by thin horizontal hairlines; a thin vertical line divides sidebar from content; the filter dropdown ("Current year") has a thin outline.
why: Helps navigate complex interfaces more easily and adds a touch of sophistication. Both techniques (colour and outline) enhance usability as well as aesthetics.
doDont: Do (thumbs-up): dashboard on white with thin, light outlines around cards and dividers between sidebar groups. Don't: leave sections unseparated (see D-11 bad example).
auditCheck: Are there flat white regions of different purpose with no separation by tone, outline or shadow? Are outline widths 1px (inference) and colour low-contrast?
restyleFix: Add `border: 1px solid <light grey>` to cards and `border-top/bottom` hairlines between sidebar groups, keeping the outline light (see D-14).

title: Don't overdo borders and background colours
rule: Don't overuse borders or multiple background colours per section. Rely on colour and generous white space to separate sections (e.g. results from buttons).
why: Overuse of borders clutters the interface and makes it busy, confusing or outdated; excess lines and colours detract from the content, make the UI overcomplicated and harder to navigate, and overwhelm the user. Smart use of white space and background colours achieves the same separation and focus without visual noise. Borders are fine when used sparingly and intentionally – find the balance.
doDont: Don't (left, thumbs-down): "Pick your flavours" modal with a divider under the title, a bordered pill search field between two full-width lines, a divider line between every flavour row (Raspberry $2.40, Apricot $2.10, Orange $1.80, Grape $1.30, Papaya $4.20), a grey-tinted footer region with a top line holding Cancel/Continue. Do (right, thumbs-up): same modal with no borders: search field uses a light grey fill, rows separated only by spacing, footer on white with generous whitespace; Continue is a filled purple pill, Cancel plain text.
auditCheck: Count borders/dividers per component; flag a divider between every list row plus section borders plus differently coloured section backgrounds in the same card. Flag a bordered input on top of a bordered/dividered header. Could the same separation be achieved with spacing or a subtle fill?
restyleFix: Remove row dividers and section borders; replace with spacing (increase vertical padding), use a light grey fill for the search input, drop footer background tint.

title: Keep borders thin and light
rule: Borders should be thin and light; subtlety is key. Avoid thick, dark or prominent borders.
why: Thick, dark, prominent borders overpower content and make the interface feel heavy and outdated. Thin, light borders define sections without stealing the spotlight, keep the aesthetic light and open, are easier on the eyes and give a more pleasant experience. "Less is often more."
doDont: Don't (thumbs-down): "Recent orders" table (columns Customer ID, Customer name, Item name, Order date, Status [Paid/Pending/Cancel pills], Price; Previous / pagination 1 2 3 … 8 9 10 / Next) with dark, full-strength row lines and dark-outlined Filter/Previous/Next buttons. Do (thumbs-up): same table with pale hairline row separators and light-grey outlines on Filter/Previous/Next buttons; the data stays the focus.
auditCheck: Border colour darker than a light grey (e.g. near-black/dark grey `#000`/`#333` borders on table rows or buttons) or width above 1px on routine dividers (no exact threshold in PDF; examples use 1px light lines).
restyleFix: Set borders to `1px solid` very light grey (low contrast with background, e.g. around #E5E7EB-level, from visual) for table rows and secondary buttons.

title: It is OK to break the border rules deliberately (e.g. bold 10px soft border)
rule: You may break the "thin and light" rule to achieve a specific style/brand image, provided the result stays balanced and the line stays smooth and soft. Example: flight search box with either a subtle 1px outline border or a bold 10px border (a soft, pale-blue translucent frame) – both are valid.
why: Both designs achieve different effects for different styles, yet both work because they maintain balance; even a thick border doesn't overpower when it is smooth and soft. It's all about balance and alignment with overall design goals; break rules thoughtfully and deliberately.
doDont: Do (both thumbs-up): (1) flight search box (Return/One way, Economy class, 1 passenger, 2 luggages; From Vienna VIE → To London STN; Departure Friday 17 June → Return Sunday 19 June; blue Search button) with a 1px outline and soft shadow; (2) same box inside a 10px soft, pale blue/pinkish blurred frame. Don't: apply a thick border that is dark/hard and overpowering (implied).
auditCheck: If a border is thick (>2px (inference)), is it soft/low-contrast and consistent with the brand style, or is it dark and harsh? Is the exception intentional and consistent across the product?
restyleFix: If a thick border is wanted, make it a translucent, low-contrast tint of the brand colour with soft edges; otherwise revert to 1px light.

title: Use glassmorphism only when it fits the brand and benefits users
rule: The glass ("glassmorphism") effect – UI elements that look like frosted/blurred glass – can add a modern, futuristic touch, depth and texture, realism and sophistication that flat designs lack. But it's not one-size-fits-all: decide whether it aligns with the brand and benefits users.
why: Can elevate the design and make it more dynamic and engaging, but may be inappropriate for some brands.
doDont: Do consider it for e.g. a SaaS company (modern, fresh). Don't force it on e.g. a luxury cosmetics brand that may prefer a traditional or minimalistic approach.
auditCheck: Is a glass/blur style present that conflicts with brand tone, or applied everywhere without purpose?
restyleFix: Apply backdrop blur/translucent fill only to selected floating components over rich imagery; keep brand-conservative products flat/minimal.

title: A flat, plain background is a valid baseline (media player on dark grey)
rule: A component on a flat, plain background is clean, readable and does its job well. Example: "Life of parrots" player (Documentary · 1 hr 3 min, 02:15 / 04:32, green progress bar, pause, volume, fullscreen icons, photo thumbnail of a scarlet macaw) as a near-black card on a flat dark grey page.
why: Clean, readable, does its job – glass is an enhancement, not a requirement.
doDont: Do (thumbs-up): opaque dark player on flat dark-grey background; high legibility of white title and grey text.
auditCheck: Where glass effect is absent and the background is plain, don't flag it as a defect; only recommend glass if it adds purpose.
restyleFix: Keep as is, or upgrade to glass (D-18) only when there is a rich image behind the component.

title: When using glass, keep text legible and the effect balanced – modern but not overbearing
rule: The glass effect should serve a purpose: elevate the visual appeal of the component so it stands out without compromising user experience; be modern but not overbearing, eye-catching but not distracting. Good example: the same player as a translucent, blurred, darkly tinted green glass panel with subtle light border over a dark, deep-green jungle photo – white title, preview text and controls remain readable.
why: Adds sophistication and high-tech allure while keeping usability.
doDont: Do (thumbs-up): glass panel over a dark jungle photo; text clearly legible. Don't (thumbs-down, no text explanation – from visual): the same glass panel over a bright, light teal/misty jungle photo; the panel is pale, white text and secondary text/progress bar lose contrast (the "Documentary · 1 hr 3 min" line, timestamps and controls become faint), so the effect becomes hard to read.
auditCheck: Measure text/control contrast on top of translucent/backdrop-blur surfaces over the brightest region of the background (WCAG AA 4.5:1 for text is the standard check; the PDF gives no number). Is the tint/blur strong enough? Does secondary text vanish on light imagery?
restyleFix: Add a darker tint (higher fill opacity) and/or stronger backdrop blur to the glass panel, or darken/overlay the background image; keep a faint 1px light border for edge definition.

title: Never put a glass (frosted/translucent) effect on a too-light background
rule: Glassmorphism can add contemporary flair but must not be used where the background behind the glass is too light; the effect must never cost readability or accessibility. Trend-following never outranks basic principles of readability/accessibility.
why: A glass layer over a light background significantly compromises accessibility and readability; it makes the UI harder to navigate and read, so the effect "detracts" instead of adding value.
doDont: Don't: third example from the previous page – glass panel on a light background, content hard to view/interact with. Do: (from the previous page's pair) use glass only where the backdrop gives enough contrast for the content on it. (Only text on this page; images of the examples are on p.64.)
auditCheck: For any element using `backdrop-filter: blur()` / translucent fill (rgba alpha < 1, Figma "background blur"), measure text/icon contrast against the *actual* backdrop behind it (WCAG 4.5:1 body text, 3:1 large text/UI (inference: thresholds not stated on p.65)). Flag light-on-light or dark-on-light-translucent combos below threshold.
restyleFix: Darken/colour the backdrop behind the glass, increase glass fill opacity or tint, or drop the glass effect and use a solid surface; ensure text colour contrasts with the blended result.

title: Pick the colour scheme for mood and brand personality
rule: Colour is functional, not just decorative: it sets mood, conveys brand personality and influences behaviour; different colours evoke different emotional responses, so choose a scheme that makes users feel comfortable/engaged/excited as intended.
why: Colour plays a fundamental role in user interaction and experience.
doDont: Intro only – no example.
auditCheck: Does the palette communicate the intended brand mood/tone? Is each colour assigned a purpose (brand, action, status, neutral) rather than picked ad hoc?
restyleFix: Define a purposeful palette (primary/brand, neutrals, status colours) and assign roles before restyling.

title: Use the primary/brand colour sparingly – reserve it for clickable elements
rule: Do not go all-out with brand/primary colours. Apply the primary colour selectively, mostly on interactive elements (buttons, links), so it works as a visual cue for where to click.
why: Overusing the primary colour overwhelms users, detracts from content, unbalances the design and makes the UI messy. "When everything is highlighted, nothing stands out"; it loses its role as a guide for interactivity.
doDont: Don't (fintech app, pink brand): pink everywhere – account header text and icon tile, big pink card, filled pink Send/Request buttons, pink contact "Add new" circle, pink section titles/"See all" links, pink nav icons (from visual). Do: same screen, pink only on the payment card and small accents (active nav dot, dashed Add-new outline); Send/Request become neutral light-grey buttons, section titles/icons neutral grey/black (from visual) – the colour then marks the focal items only.
auditCheck: Count how much of the screen area/elements use the primary hue; are non-interactive things (headings, icons, labels, decorative blocks) coloured with the action colour? Rule of thumb: if primary colour appears on many non-clickable elements or on more than a few focal elements per screen (inference), flag. Can a user tell clickable from non-clickable by colour alone?
restyleFix: Move primary colour to the main CTAs/links/active states only; switch headings, secondary icons, secondary buttons to neutrals (greys/near-black); keep at most one or two highlighted focal items.

title: Keep the overall palette balanced – don't use too many colours
rule: Beyond restraint with the primary colour, keep the whole colour scheme balanced; too many different colours is as harmful as overusing one.
why: Too many colours cause visual clutter and make it hard to know where to focus.
doDont: Text only. Don't: many competing hues on one screen. Do: a small, balanced scheme.
auditCheck: Count distinct non-neutral hues used on a screen (excluding status colours/data viz); flag if more than ~1 brand hue + 1 accent (the PDF gives no number – threshold is an inference) or if hues have no assigned role.
restyleFix: Collapse to one primary hue (+ optional accent) and neutrals; map remaining colours to neutral shades or status roles.

title: Use neutral backgrounds (grey, beige, soft white), not vibrant ones
rule: Default to neutral backgrounds — shades of grey, beige, or soft whites — as a clean canvas so content and primary colours pop without competing.
why: Neutral backgrounds make it easier to focus on tasks/absorb information. Vibrant backgrounds clash with text and other UI elements, reduce readability, feel less clear and overwhelming, worsening UX even though they look "dynamic or creative" at first glance.
doDont: Don't (portfolio screen): saturated deep-violet/indigo full-screen background with purple tab bar; coloured chart rings, text and list all sit on it and clash/compete (from visual). Do: same screen on near-white/very light grey background; chart rings and pink "See more" link pop; text easy to read; neutral backdrop minimises distraction.
auditCheck: Is the main page/screen background a saturated colour (high chroma, e.g. HSL saturation > ~50% (inference; PDF gives no number) – limit to light/mid lightness (about 25-75%) (inference); dark navy surfaces recommended in E-07 are fine) rather than white/grey/beige? Do charts/accents/text compete with it?
restyleFix: Replace the page/screen background with white/off-white/light grey (or beige); move brand colour to accents/CTAs; confine saturated fills to small areas.

title: Reserve coloured backgrounds for splash screens, headers and specialised sections
rule: Coloured backgrounds can work beautifully, but only in specific places: splash screens, headers, or specialised sections of an app/site. Know when and where to introduce colour so it adds to the experience.
why: Used in the right spot it enhances; used as the general background it detracts (see E-05).
doDont: Text only. Do: colour hero/header/splash/special band. Don't: colour the whole content area.
auditCheck: Is a saturated background used on content-heavy/working screens or full pages rather than on a header/hero/splash/feature section?
restyleFix: Limit the coloured background to a hero/header/section band; keep content areas neutral.

title: Dark backgrounds are a valid, beneficial option
rule: Dark backgrounds are not just a trend; they give visually appealing contrast that makes text and elements pop, and are easier on the eyes in low light. Light text on dark reduces glare and flicker and lessens eye strain over extended use.
why: Engaging, readable UI; reduced eye strain in low-light/extended use.
doDont: Both examples are marked "good" (thumbs-up): same portfolio screen on a near-black/dark navy background with light text and coloured rings (soft white text, not pure) and on a light background (from visual).
auditCheck: If a dark theme exists, are surfaces dark neutral (not saturated) with light text and clear contrast? Does it keep the same hierarchy as light?
restyleFix: Provide a dark neutral palette (very dark navy/grey surfaces, light text, same accent colours) instead of a vibrant background.

title: Offer dark mode as a user-switchable option
rule: Provide a light/dark switch; dark mode is now a must-have for many users, not a nice-to-have.
why: Caters to a broader range of preferences and needs; makes the UI inclusive and versatile.
doDont: Text only (the p.69 image shows the same screen in both modes).
auditCheck: Does the product offer a dark theme / respect `prefers-color-scheme`? Are colours defined as theme tokens so both themes exist?
restyleFix: Define semantic colour tokens with light and dark values; add a theme toggle / honour system setting.

title: Choose light vs dark to fit UX and brand image
rule: The light/dark choice should consider UX and align with the brand's image; whether crisp white or moody dark, it must complement the overall aesthetic and message.
why: Background is part of brand expression.
doDont: Text only.
auditCheck: Does the default theme match brand tone/audience context?
restyleFix: Select default theme (white vs moody dark) deliberately according to brand message.

title: Don't rely on colour alone to convey state – add icon, label or pattern
rule: For errors, success, warnings, combine colour with other cues: icons, text labels, patterns. Example: red field border + exclamation-mark icon + message "Enter amount bigger than $1".
why: Bright red may not convey error/urgency to all users, especially those with colour-vision deficiencies or viewing in different lighting conditions.
doDont: Don't: "Sale amount $ 0.01 USD" input with only a red/coral border (no icon, no message). Do: same input with red border + red "!" circle icon inside the field (before the USD selector) + red helper text "Enter amount bigger than $1" below.
auditCheck: For each error/success/warning state, is there at least one non-colour indicator (icon AND/OR text message)? Check that state is distinguishable in greyscale. Flag fields that change only border/background colour.
restyleFix: Add a status icon and a short explanatory message next to the coloured state; keep colour as reinforcement.

title: Use conventional colours for system statuses (red=error, green=success)
rule: When using colour for statuses, stick to widely accepted conventions: red for stop/error, green for go/success. Don't use yellow for errors or pink for success, even if it matches the brand.
why: Conventions come from years of user interaction and design studies; breaking them creates confusion and slows interaction because people must think twice about your custom colour coding.
doDont: Error – Don't: yellow/amber border, icon and message on the "Sale amount" field; Do: red/coral border, icon and message. Success – Don't: pink border and check icon on "Email olivia@untitledui.com"; Do: green border and green check icon.
auditCheck: Are error/danger states red-hued, success green-hued, (warning amber/yellow by convention)? Flag brand-colour or off-convention status colours (e.g. amber errors, pink/blue success).
restyleFix: Recolour statuses to red (error) / green (success) / amber (warning); keep icons + text.

title: Fit status colours to the brand via tone, not hue
rule: To harmonise status colours with the brand, vary the *tones* (shade/tint/saturation) of the conventional colours rather than replacing them with brand colours.
why: Convention is the one area where it's better to stick to what people know; tone tweaks keep recognisability while matching the palette.
doDont: Text only. Do: a brand-tuned red/green. Don't: switch the hue.
auditCheck: Is the status colour still clearly in the red/green hue families after brand adjustments? (check hue not shifted to brand colour)
restyleFix: Adjust lightness/saturation of the red/green tokens to match palette; keep hue family.

title: Choose a serif typeface for formal sectors (law, accounting, education)
rule: Pick a font like an outfit: appropriate, comfortable, effective for the message. In formal sectors (law, accounting, education) use a serif typeface for a classic, polished tone.
why: Typeface conveys tone for the sector.
doDont: Example "Faircase – Fair and Square." law-firm landing page: serif logo, nav, large serif headline, serif body and stats ("1542 Cases / 53 Lawyers / 726 Connections"), dark red/maroon CTA, tan background panel with portrait photo (from visual).
auditCheck: Does the typeface personality match the sector/brand (formal sector with playful/techy font = mismatch)?
restyleFix: Swap to a classic serif (e.g. Merriweather-like, from visual) for headings/body in formal contexts.

title: Consider a script/handwritten typeface for relaxed, personal sectors like beauty
rule: For beauty and similar relaxed, inviting sectors, a script typeface can be experimented with to feel warm and personalised.
why: Warm, personalised mood.
doDont: Example "EVELIA" skincare: light handwriting-style headline "Essential skincare collection / UP TO 70% OFF", spaced small-caps sans nav, cream background, product photos (from visual). Script is used for headline only; small text stays plain sans (from visual).
auditCheck: If a script font is used, is it restricted to display/headline text and still legible? Is it appropriate for the sector?
restyleFix: Use script for the hero headline only; keep body/UI text in a simple readable font.

title: Use sans-serif for tech, music-streaming, messaging apps
rule: In tech, music streaming and messaging contexts, sans-serif fonts are the go-to for a sleek modern aesthetic.
why: Resonates with those industries.
doDont: Example "Tucard" dark landing page: geometric sans headline "Simplify All Transactions in One Card" (with "One Card" in magenta), sans nav, small body, stats "42K+ / 12K+", glass-like cards (from visual).
auditCheck: Does a tech/app product use a decorative or serif face where sans is expected?
restyleFix: Switch to a clean sans-serif (Inter/Manrope-like).

title: Pick a font that is both readable and aesthetically pleasing
rule: Font selection is about clarity and readability as well as beauty: choose a font that is easy to read, looks good and matches the intended vibe. Avoid decorative/novelty faces for titles, body and buttons.
why: A poorly chosen font becomes the "Achilles heel" – message hard to get across, users frustrated.
doDont: Don't: article card with blackletter/gothic-style headline and condensed quirky body and button font (from visual) – hard to read. Do: same card with clean serif headline ("The Art of Achieving Success: Unveiling the Secret Ingredients to a Fulfilling Life"), plain sans body and "Learn more" button.
auditCheck: Any display/decorative/blackletter/condensed font used for body text, buttons or UI labels? Is x-height/legibility ok at body size?
restyleFix: Replace with a neutral legible text typeface; keep decorative faces (if at all) for a logo.

title: Prefer proven, versatile UI fonts
rule: Reliable "good in any situation" fonts that balance style with readability: Inter, Gotham, Lato, Open Sans, San Francisco, Helvetica, Manrope, Roboto.
why: They are trusted, readable all-rounders.
doDont: List only.
auditCheck: Is the primary font among well-tested UI typefaces (or equivalent quality)?
restyleFix: Default to one of these list fonts when no brand font exists.

title: Only use properly licensed fonts (Google Fonts for free)
rule: Make sure the font can be used for personal or commercial purposes as your project requires; never use fonts without proper license. Google Fonts is a reliable source of free, safe fonts.
why: Legal/licensing safety.
doDont: Text only.
auditCheck: Are fonts self-hosted/loaded from a licensed source (Google Fonts, purchased licence)? Flag unlicensed commercial fonts (e.g. ripped webfonts).
restyleFix: Replace with an open-licensed (Google Fonts) alternative.

title: Use at most 2 different fonts per UI
rule: Never use more than two font families. More than two looks cluttered, confusing and off-brand.
why: Messy and harder to look at; one or two fonts feel clean.
doDont: Don't: music app screen with four families – Poppins (title) + Open Sans (subtitle), Times (track titles), Telex (button, UPPERCASE "DISCOVER MORE"). Do: same screen all Inter ("Music", "Special edition", track titles, "Discover more").
auditCheck: Count distinct `font-family` values (excluding icon/mono fallbacks) in CSS/Figma text styles: > 2 → flag.
restyleFix: Consolidate to 1 (ideally) or 2 families; remap all text styles.

title: Best practice: one versatile font, vary weight and size for dynamics
rule: For a clean, professional look, stick to one versatile font and create dynamics via different weights and sizes.
why: Cleaner and more professional.
doDont: Do: all-Inter example (see E-19).
auditCheck: Is hierarchy built with weight/size in a single family rather than extra families?
restyleFix: Replace secondary family with a different weight/size of the primary family.

title: If using two fonts: one for headings, one for body, from proven pairings
rule: Experienced designers can use two fonts: one for headings, another for paragraphs. Pairs named: Playfair Display (headings) + Sources Sans Pro (body); Raleway + Merriweather; Montserrat + Open Sans. Figma's curated pairing list: www.figma.com/google-fonts.
why: A classic combo that adds range without clutter.
doDont: Text only.
auditCheck: If two families exist, is the split by role (heading vs body) and are they a deliberate contrasting pair?
restyleFix: Assign one family to headings, the other to body; use a pair from the list.

title: Keep body-copy line length at 45-75 characters on desktop
rule: For body copy on desktop, line length should be 45-75 characters per line (research-backed sweet spot). These are guidelines, not strict rules.
why: Optimises readability/visual appeal; keeps focus and prevents users feeling overwhelmed or losing their place.
doDont: Diagram with ruler markers 0, 20, 45, 75, 100 characters in a browser frame. Green (good) text blocks: one spanning to ~75, another ending at roughly 45 (from visual). Pink (bad) blocks: a narrow block of ~20 characters per line (too short, choppy) and a wide block running out to ~100 characters (too long).
auditCheck: Measure real characters per line of the rendered body paragraph (browser: `Range.getClientRects()` per line plus the line's text length; or font metrics) – do not infer it from a `ch` value: 1ch is the width of the `0` glyph, not an average character (one proportional UI font measured 72ch ≈ 93 real characters per line, while 36em ≈ 73.5; inference from a real-project measurement). Flag if >75 or <45 on desktop (e.g. no `max-width` on a paragraph in a wide container, `max-w-none`, full-width text).
restyleFix: Cap the column in `em`/`rem`; rule of thumb for proportional UI fonts about 30–36em gives 45–75 characters (inference – 36em ≈ 73.5 characters in one measured font, about 2.0 characters/em; verify per font by re-measuring). Use `ch` only for monospace fonts. Centre or left-align the constrained column; `max-w-prose` (65ch) is not a safe shortcut for proportional fonts.

title: On mobile aim for 30-40 characters per line
rule: On mobile, the rule of thumb is 30 to 40 characters per line.
why: Smaller screens; keeps text easily digestible without hurting readability.
doDont: Text only.
auditCheck: At mobile widths, count real characters per line of body copy (measure rendered lines, not `ch`): outside ~30-40 (guideline) → check.
restyleFix: Adjust horizontal padding / font-size so mobile lines land at 30-40 chars.

title: Measure line length with tools instead of counting
rule: Use Figma plugins like "Character counter" or online tools to check characters per line.
why: Avoid manual counting.
doDont: Text only.
auditCheck: Tooling note – measure via plugin/JS: per-line `Range.getClientRects()` with the text of each line, or font metrics; a width ÷ "average character width" guess or a `ch` conversion is not a measurement (1ch = width of `0`).
restyleFix: n/a (process tip).

title: Allow flexibility in line length by content, layout and device
rule: 45-75 chars is not one-size-fits-all; depending on content, layout, or target device some flexibility is beneficial.
why: Context changes ideal measure.
doDont: Text only.
auditCheck: Deviations from 45-75 should be justified (e.g. mobile 30-40, short UI captions).
restyleFix: Tune per breakpoint.

title: Don't let body text span the full page width
rule: Text stretching across the whole page width is hard to read; constrain it.
why: Eyes must travel a long distance from end of one line to start of next, increasing eye strain and reducing readability.
doDont: Don't: dog-community landing page – below the hero, heading "Why people love dogs" and a paragraph running the full container width (~100+ characters per line, 4 lines), small grey text (from visual).
auditCheck: Paragraph container whose rendered lines exceed ~75 real characters (measure per line in the browser, see E-22; do not convert from `ch`, since 1ch is the width of `0`, not an average character) with long unbroken lines.
restyleFix: Add a `max-width` that yields ≤ 75 real characters per line; for proportional UI fonts about 30–36em is a starting point (inference – verify per font).

title: Narrow centered text column (≤75 chars) is a valid fix
rule: Center-align the text *block* below the image/intro and limit line length to max 75 characters.
why: Eyes travel less, easier to move from line end to next line start.
doDont: Do: paragraph block ("Why people love dogs", 4 lines at ~70 chars) is a narrower column positioned in the centre of the container; the heading is left-aligned with the paragraph inside the column (from visual – the block is centred, text itself remains left-aligned).
auditCheck: Text block in wide container is constrained to ≤75 real characters per line (measure it, see E-22) and centred (`mx-auto max-w-…`).
restyleFix: Wrap in centred container with max-width ≈75 characters.

title: Narrow left-aligned text column (≤75 chars) is the other valid fix
rule: Left-align the text with line length not exceeding 75 characters for a traditional, straightforward feel.
why: Restricted line length makes text easily digestible, reduces eye strain.
doDont: Do: paragraph (6 lines) left-aligned with the page's hero text left edge, block ends well before the right side of the container (from visual), leaving empty space at right.
auditCheck: Left-aligned body text with measure ≤75 characters, aligned to the same left edge as the heading/hero content.
restyleFix: Set a max-width that gives ≤75 real characters per line (about 30–36em for proportional UI fonts, inference – verify per font; `ch` only for monospace), keep left alignment with the hero's left edge.

title: Break long paragraphs into shorter chunks
rule: In content-heavy sections use shorter paragraphs; split long blocks into bite-sized chunks with visible space between them.
why: Long blocks overwhelm users, hard to absorb and stay engaged; breaks make content easier to scan/digest, give natural stopping points, highlight crucial info, make reading more interactive.
doDont: Don't: "GreenMeal" card with one dense ~9-line paragraph block. Do: same text split into three short paragraphs (~3-4 lines each) with a blank gap (paragraph spacing) between them.
auditCheck: Paragraphs longer than ~5-6 lines (≈ 80-100 words – inferred) without breaks; no margin between paragraphs.
restyleFix: Split at sentence/idea boundaries; add paragraph spacing (e.g. ~0.75-1em, inferred).

title: Add subheadings (with icons/lines/space) to shorter paragraphs
rule: Give each short paragraph a subheading – a roadmap to the content. Make sections stand out further with icons, lines (dividers) or extra space.
why: Subheadings make text scannable, grab attention, preview the paragraph, and break information into digestible parts.
doDont: Don't: card titled "GreenMeal" with one dense paragraph. Do: card titled "GreenMeal: your healthy dining partner" containing three sections, each with an emoji-icon + bold subheading ("Organic ingredients for optimal nutrition", "Unlock a world of culinary delights", "Customize to fit your lifestyle") followed by a short paragraph, thin divider lines between sections and extra spacing; the main title is bigger/bolder than subheadings, which are bolder than body (from visual).
auditCheck: Text sections > 1 paragraph or long copy without subheads; subheads present but not visually distinct (same size/weight as body).
restyleFix: Add descriptive subheadings (semibold, slightly larger than body), optional icons, dividers (1px light line) and increased spacing between sections.

title: Avoid pure black (#000000) text on white, and pure white (#FFFFFF) on dark
rule: Don't use #000000 text on white backgrounds or #FFFFFF text on dark backgrounds. Use off-black/dark grey for headings and a lighter grey for body text.
why: Pure extremes are hard on the eyes and disrupt visual harmony; a softer scheme is soothing, sophisticated and balanced; dark grey headings say "this is significant" without screaming; lighter grey text stays readable without overwhelming.
doDont: Don't: dark card Heading #FFFFFF / Body #FFFFFF on black; light card Heading #000000 / Body #000000 on white. Do: see E-32.
auditCheck: Grep CSS/tokens for `color: #000`, `#000000`, `black`, `#fff`/`#ffffff`/`white` used as text colour on respective extremes (`text-black`, `text-white` on `bg-black`/`bg-white`/very dark).
restyleFix: Replace with off-black/dark-grey tokens and lighter grey body (E-32 values).

title: Use graded greys: darker heading, lighter body text (reference values)
rule: Heading darker/stronger than body text, both soft. Reference values from the example — Dark mode (on black background): heading #F2F2F2, body #CACACA. Light mode (on white background): heading #1A1A1A, body #4E4E4E.
why: Refined contrast "that just feels right" while keeping a heading/body hierarchy.
doDont: Do: example "The scoop on ice cream" card in both DARK and LIGHT variants using values above; heading visibly brighter/darker than body. Don't: identical colour for heading and body (#FFFFFF/#FFFFFF, #000000/#000000).
auditCheck: Heading and body use different, non-extreme colours; light theme text ≈ #1A1A1A heading / ≈ #4E4E4E body (contrast of #4E4E4E on white = 8.32:1 – computed, still above WCAG AA); dark theme ≈ #F2F2F2 / ≈ #CACACA. Flag body greys lighter than AA 4.5:1 (inference: threshold not on p.83).
restyleFix: Set text tokens: light — heading #1A1A1A, body #4E4E4E; dark — heading #F2F2F2, body #CACACA.

title: Use heavier weights for headings and lighter for body
rule: Headings: bold, semibold or medium; paragraphs: regular, sometimes light. Don't use the same weight for heading and body.
why: Weight adds visual interest and tells users what is most important; thin body weights stay readable and don't compete with headings.
doDont: Don't: card "The canine connection" with heading Regular and body Regular – hard to tell what's important. Do: heading Bold, body Regular – clear what to focus on and what to skim.
auditCheck: Compare `font-weight` of headings vs body: equal (e.g. 400/400) → flag. Headings should be ≥500 (medium/semibold/bold), body 300-400.
restyleFix: Set headings to 500-700 and body to 400 (or 300).

title: Light-weight headings are acceptable only if clearly larger than body (colour reinforces)
section: Typography: exceptions and extremes to avoid (p.85-87)
rule: Modern sites (Pleo, Linear) use light/regular font weights for headings and still get clear hierarchy, because they do not rely on weight alone: headings use a darker colour than paragraphs (paragraphs lighter) and, above all, headings are set noticeably larger than the rest of the text. If you break the "bold headings" convention, size (mostly) + colour must compensate.
why: Hierarchy comes from combined contrast of size, colour and weight; size contrast is the strongest, so a big heading stays dominant even at light weight.
doDont: Do (Pleo hero screenshot, from visual): large, light-weight dark headline "Your business spending, in safe hands" over smaller, greyer paragraph and a dark pill CTA. Don't: use a light heading weight with heading size ≈ body size and same colour.
auditCheck: Is any heading using weight < medium (≤400)? If yes, it is acceptable only when its size is clearly larger than body text (visually unmistakable) – size is what p.85 says these sites rely on MOST. A darker heading colour vs body (lighter paragraphs) is a reinforcement that helps, not a substitute. Light-weight heading that is not clearly larger than body → hierarchy is lost, flag it, even if its colour is darker than body.
restyleFix: Either raise heading weight to medium/semibold/bold, or keep light weight but increase heading font-size substantially and darken heading colour relative to paragraph colour.

title: Never use text colour that is too light (light-grey text)
section: Typography: exceptions and extremes to avoid (p.85-87)
rule: Don't set text in very light grey in the name of minimalism. Example pair: body text `#A9A9A9` on white = fails WCAG AA and AAA (bad); body text `#626262` on white = passes WCAG AA and AAA (good, per the PDF's badge). **[ux-doctor erratum: #626262 on white computes to 6.1:1 = AA pass only; AAA normal text needs 7:1. Use computed values.]** Keep text dark enough to pass contrast (see F-09).
why: Light-grey text forces squinting/tilting the screen (e.g. reading on a phone in a coffee shop), hurts users with poorer vision.
doDont: Same card (image of yellow fish, heading + 5-line paragraph). Bad card: paragraph #A9A9A9, badge "WCAG AA: Fail / WCAG AAA: Fail". Good card: paragraph #626262, "WCAG AA: Pass / WCAG AAA: Pass". Heading is near-black in both.
auditCheck: Compute contrast of every text colour vs its background; flag body text lighter than ~#767676-equivalent (inference) / below 4.5:1 (the PDF shows #A9A9A9 failing and #626262 passing). Look for Tailwind `text-gray-300/400`, `opacity-50` on text, placeholder-grey used for content.
restyleFix: Darken paragraph/secondary text to at least ~#626262 on white (or any value giving ≥4.5:1); keep it lighter than headings to preserve hierarchy.

title: Avoid extra-light (thin) font weights for body text
section: Typography: exceptions and extremes to avoid (p.85-87)
rule: Stick to regular or medium weights for the bulk of text. Avoid Extra-light / Thin (e.g. Inter Extra Light, Inter Thin).
why: Thin strokes blend into the background or break apart, especially on small screens or poor lighting; hurts older adults and visually impaired users.
doDont: Same coral-reef card twice. Bad: paragraph in "Font-weight: Extra-light" (faint, thin). Good: "Font-weight: Regular". Heading is semibold in both.
auditCheck: Any body/paragraph `font-weight` < 400 (100/200 especially; Tailwind `font-thin`, `font-extralight`)? Flag. `font-light` (300) on small text is a warning (inference).
restyleFix: Set body to `font-weight: 400` (or 500 if the font is delicate/small).

title: Use size to signal which text is important
rule: Size is the most direct way to establish hierarchy; bigger elements attract more attention. Make the message that matters most the largest.
why: Users read the biggest text first; if the wrong text is biggest they act on the wrong message (analogy: giant "Start the engine and go full speed" vs. small "Wait until you see the green light!" at a red light → crash).
doDont: Two cards with a traffic-light image. Bad: "Wait until you see the green light!" tiny, "Start the engine and go full speed" large. Good: "Wait until you see the green light!" large, "Start the engine and go full speed" small.
auditCheck: Is the largest text on each card/section the one the user most needs to see (primary message, warning, key value)? Is a secondary/optional/ancillary text larger than the critical one?
restyleFix: Re-assign type scale so the most important text gets the largest size and secondary text is reduced.

title: Make headings clearly bigger than body text
rule: A heading must be much larger than body text. Even with the same colours and fonts, a bigger heading alone creates clear hierarchy and contrast; a title the same size as regular text makes it hard to tell what is important and doesn't attract attention.
why: Without size contrast users can't scan for importance and may not be drawn to read on.
doDont: Watch-promo card (serif font, same colours). Good (first card): large two-line heading "Timeless elegance watch edition", small paragraph, small black "Get it today" button. Bad (second card): heading "Timeless elegance watch edition" at the same small size as the paragraph, single line.
auditCheck: heading font-size ÷ body font-size ≈ 1? (heading ≈ body size = violation). Compare computed sizes of h1/h2/card titles vs paragraph.
restyleFix: Increase heading size to a clear step up (compare example p.95: 28px heading vs 18px body ≈ 1.55x; p.90: 32px title vs 16px body = 2x).

title: Use readable font sizes: 16px for main text, never below ~12px (10px floor)
rule: The "gold standard" for main/body copy is 16px (sweet spot for most people). Can be tweaked by platform or typeface. Avoid anything below 12px for main text; the "things to avoid" list says no font sizes smaller than 10px (platform-dependent). When in doubt test on different devices and with other people.
why: Small text is hard to decipher, can make users bounce, and creates accessibility problems for visually impaired users.
doDont: "Sea turtles" card with tabs (All / Life / Early years / Special skills). Bad card: title 32px, tabs 16px, body paragraph 10px (tiny, long text). Good card: title 32px, tabs 16px, body paragraph 16px.
auditCheck: Main text `font-size` < 12px = violation (p.90: "anything below 12px for main text should be avoided"). Any text < 10px = violation, but platform-dependent (p.96: "smaller than 10px, though this can depend on the platform"). Body < 16px = check, not automatic fail (inference): p.90 calls 16px the "gold standard" but "not a one-size-fits-all rule". (Tailwind `text-[10px]`; `text-xs` = 12px is at the limit when used for main text.) Check on mobile too.
restyleFix: Set body copy to 16px (adjust for platform/typeface); raise any 10px content text to ≥12px, preferably 16px.

title: Use generous line-height for body text: 1.5-1.6x (150-160%)
rule: For standard ~16px text, line-height should be 1.5-1.6x the font size (150%-160%). Above 2x paragraphs look like they float; below 1.2x text feels cramped.
why: Comfortable reading without text looking squished or stretched; the same font/size/colour can go from "meh" to "wow" by line-height alone.
doDont: "The magic of coffee" card twice, identical font/size/colour. Bad: tightly packed lines (cramped). Good: more open spacing between lines.
auditCheck: Paragraph `line-height` ratio: <1.2 = fail (cramped); 1.2-1.5 = weak (inference); 1.5-1.6 = ideal; >2 = fail (floating). Tailwind `leading-none/tight` on paragraphs = violation.
restyleFix: Set paragraph `line-height: 1.5`-`1.6` (e.g. `leading-relaxed`/1.6 for 16px).

title: Tighter line-height for headings, looser for paragraphs
rule: Line-height should scale inversely with text size: bigger text → smaller line-height ratio. Headings use tight line-height (example 120%; a 36px heading → about 1.3x / 130%), paragraphs use generous (160%). Never give a heading a bigger line-height than the paragraph.
why: Tight headings look compact and impactful ("this is important"); open paragraphs are inviting and easier to read; creates balanced visual flow and easier scanning.
doDont: "Unveiling the wonders…" card. Bad: heading Line-height 160% and paragraph Line-height 120% (inverted: airy heading, cramped body). Good: heading 120%, paragraph 160%.
auditCheck: Compare the computed heading line-height ratio with the paragraph ratio of the same context. Violation = heading line-height ≥ paragraph line-height (playbook: never bigger), or heading lines visibly colliding/clipped (inference). The heading ratio shrinks as size grows (playbook: 120% in the card example, ~1.3 for a 36px heading), so a fixed "> 1.3" cut-off is not a failure test: large display type (≥ ~56px) at 1.0–1.15 is not a violation by itself (inference), and a 1.3 multi-line heading beside 1.6 body passes.
restyleFix: Headings `line-height` ≈ 1.2-1.3; paragraphs 1.5-1.6.

title: Ensure text/background contrast of at least 4.5:1 (WCAG AA)
rule: For most text a contrast ratio ≥ 4.5:1 is accessible; designs should meet at least WCAG Level AA. Don't use faint text on a similarly faint background for trendiness; never use bad contrast solely for an aesthetic look. Tools: WebAIM guides, Coolors.co, Figma "Contrast" plugin by WillowTree.
why: Trendy low-contrast designs are hard to read for people with vision difficulty or in bad lighting; put readability first.
doDont: "The Pawsome World of Dogs" card with purple/lilac background. Bad: white/light text on lilac → "WCAG AA: Fail, AAA: Fail". Good: dark purple/near-black heading and body text on same lilac background → AA Pass, AAA Pass.
auditCheck: Contrast ratio of each text/background pair < 4.5:1 → fail (normal text). Check text over tinted/coloured card backgrounds and over images.
restyleFix: Darken text (or lighten/darken background) until ≥4.5:1; on mid-tone coloured backgrounds use dark text instead of white.

title: Left-align text; reserve centre/right for special cases
rule: Left-aligned text is generally best for readability, especially longer paragraphs, lists and long-form content (consistent starting point per line; matches left-to-right reading). Centre alignment is OK for titles or short text meant to grab attention, and right/centre for decorative or artistic elements.
why: Consistent line start makes it easier to follow lines; ragged left edges slow reading.
doDont: Dark navy "The Critical Role of Sleep…" card twice. Bad: heading and paragraph centred ("Text alignment: Center"). Good: heading and paragraph left-aligned ("Text alignment: Left").
auditCheck: `text-align: center|right` (Tailwind `text-center`/`text-right`) on multi-line paragraphs (>2-3 lines (inference)), lists or long descriptions → violation. Centre on short titles/hero lines OK.
restyleFix: Set `text-align: left` (`text-left`) on body paragraphs and multi-line copy; keep centre only for short titles.

title: Worked example: bad vs good typography card (full spec)
rule: Combine all principles on one card. Good card spec: heading line-height 120%, font-size 28px, weight Bold, colour `#1B000D` (near-black with tint); body line-height 160%, font-size 18px, weight Regular, colour `#5E5458` (softer than heading); button label font-size 18px, weight Semibold, colour `#141B12`; left-aligned text; WCAG AA and AAA Pass. Bad card spec: heading line-height 170%, 22px, Medium, `#000000`; body line-height 110%, 18px, Regular, `#000000`; button label 22px, Regular, `#FFFFFF` on pink; centre-aligned; button label WCAG AA Fail / AAA Fail.
why: Line height, contrast, weight, size and colour differences together make text more readable and engaging ("elevate design from good to great").
doDont: Card with Japan illustration, title "Exploring the land of the rising sun: A journey through Japan's rich culture and history", paragraph, pink "Learn more →" button. Bad: centred text; heading only 22px (barely > 18px body), medium weight, pure black; heading line-height 170% vs body 110% (inverted); pure black body (same as heading); white button label on pink fails contrast. Good: left-aligned; heading 28px bold, tight 120%; body 18px regular grey-brown, loose 160%; heading darker than body; dark semibold button label on pink passes.
auditCheck: Test each point: heading/body size gap (28 vs 18 ≈ 1.55x), heading weight > body weight, heading darker than body, heading LH < body LH, pure #000/#FFF not used, button label contrast passes, paragraph left-aligned.
restyleFix: Apply the good spec: heading 28/120% bold `#1B000D`; body 18/160% regular `#5E5458`; button text semibold dark (`#141B12`) on light-mid pink; left-align.

title: Check button-label contrast on coloured buttons (white on pink fails)
rule: (From visual) A white (#FFFFFF), 22px Regular label on the pink "Learn more" button fails WCAG AA and AAA; a dark (#141B12) 18px Semibold label on the same pink passes both.
why: Light text on light/mid-saturated fills lacks contrast.
doDont: Bad: white regular label on pink. Good: dark semibold label on pink.
auditCheck: Measure label vs button-fill contrast ≥4.5:1; especially white text on pastel/pink/yellow/light-green buttons.
restyleFix: Switch the label to a near-black (e.g. #141B12) and increase to semibold, or darken the button fill.

title: Don't use pure black (#000000) or pure white (#FFFFFF) for both headings and paragraphs
section: Typography: "Things to avoid" and "Things to do" checklists (p.96-97)
rule: Avoid pure #000000 / #FFFFFF as the colour of both headings and paragraphs. (Good card in p.95 uses #1B000D for headings and #5E5458 for paragraph instead of #000000 for both.)
why: Using the same extreme colour everywhere removes differentiation between content types (and is the failing pattern in the p.95 bad card).
doDont: Don't #000 text everywhere (bad card). Do slightly tinted near-black for headings, softer grey for paragraphs.
auditCheck: Text colour == #000000 or #FFFFFF for both heading and body (`text-black`, `text-white` on both) → flag.
restyleFix: Heading → near-black tint (e.g. #1B000D); body → softer dark grey (e.g. #5E5458) that still passes 4.5:1. On dark mode use off-white for headings and a dimmer light-grey for paragraphs (extension of rule, not stated).

title: Use darker colour for headings and lighter colour for paragraphs
section: Typography: "Things to avoid" and "Things to do" checklists (p.96-97)
rule: Differentiate content types: headings in darker colour, paragraphs in lighter colour (but still accessible). Avoid the same colour for headings and paragraphs.
why: Guides the user's eye and distinguishes types of content.
doDont: Do heading #1B000D vs paragraph #5E5458 (p.95). Don't same colour (#000000 both).
auditCheck: Heading colour == paragraph colour → violation. Lightness gap should be visible while paragraph still ≥4.5:1.
restyleFix: Introduce a secondary text token for paragraphs lighter than the heading token.

title: Use thicker weights for headings and thinner weights for paragraphs
section: Typography: "Things to avoid" and "Things to do" checklists (p.96-97)
rule: Headings: bold, semibold or medium. Paragraphs: regular (sometimes light). Do not use the same weight for headings and paragraphs.
why: Clearly distinguishes hierarchical elements.
doDont: Do heading Bold / paragraph Regular (p.95 good card). Don't heading and paragraph at same weight (bad card heading Medium vs body Regular is the weak case; hierarchy relies on size).
auditCheck: heading `font-weight` ≤ body `font-weight` → violation (see F-01 exception if the heading is clearly larger than body). Body weight < 400 → see F-03.
restyleFix: Headings 500-700, body 400.

title: Don't give headings a bigger line-height than paragraphs (checklist form)
section: Typography: "Things to avoid" and "Things to do" checklists (p.96-97)
rule: "Things to avoid": bigger line-height for headings than for paragraphs. "Things to do": smaller line-height for headings and larger for paragraphs for balanced visual flow and easier scanning. (Detail and numbers in F-08.)
why: Balanced flow, easier scanning.
doDont: Heading 120% / paragraph 160% good; heading 160-170% / paragraph 110-120% bad.
auditCheck: heading LH ratio > paragraph LH ratio.
restyleFix: See F-08.

title: Use sans-serif typefaces for body copy
section: Typography: "Things to avoid" and "Things to do" checklists (p.96-97)
rule: Prefer sans-serif for body copy: Open Sans, Inter, Roboto are generally more readable than serifs such as Times New Roman or Georgia. Fonts can still define the brand, but readability comes first.
why: Readability.
doDont: Do Open Sans / Inter / Roboto body. Don't Times New Roman / Georgia for body text. (Serif headings, e.g. Playfair Display, are acceptable per F-18.)
auditCheck: Body `font-family` resolves to a serif (Times New Roman, Georgia, `font-serif`) → flag.
restyleFix: Switch body to Inter / Open Sans / Roboto; keep serif only for display headings if brand demands.

title: Use no more than two fonts (ideally one family with weights and sizes)
section: Typography: "Things to avoid" and "Things to do" checklists (p.96-97)
rule: Max two different fonts. Best practice: one font with different weights and sizes. Experienced designers can pair two, e.g. Playfair Display for headings + Roboto for paragraphs. Avoid fonts that compromise aesthetics or readability.
why: Consistency, readability and aesthetics.
doDont: Do one family (or a deliberate heading/body pair). Don't use 3+ typefaces or decorative fonts that hurt readability.
auditCheck: Count distinct `font-family` values in the CSS/Figma styles: >2 → violation. Check any display/script font used for body or UI labels.
restyleFix: Consolidate to a single family (e.g. Inter) using weight/size for hierarchy; or a max of one heading font + one body font.

title: Give long text blocks adequate space between paragraphs
section: Typography: "Things to avoid" and "Things to do" checklists (p.96-97)
rule: Ensure longer text blocks have adequate space between paragraphs so they look more appealing and are easier to read. (No numeric value given.)
why: Visual appeal and readability.
doDont: Do clear paragraph gaps. Don't run paragraphs together with no/very little margin.
auditCheck:
Paragraph `margin-bottom` / gap between `

` ≈ 0 in long-form text → violation.
restyleFix: Add paragraph spacing (e.g. around one line-height; value is my suggestion, not stated).

title: Minimise interaction cost (mental + physical + time effort)
rule: Interaction cost = the mental, physical and time effort a user must invest to reach their goal with a UI. A well-designed site/app reduces it. Ideal = zero (users find what they want immediately) but usually unfeasible because of feature breadth. Diagram: green straight arrow User → Goal (ideal) vs pink zig-zag path with many detours (high interaction cost).
why: Every unit of effort is friction between the user and their goal.
doDont: Do give the shortest, most direct path. Don't force detours (zig-zag).
auditCheck: For each key task, count clicks/keystrokes/scrolls/page loads/decisions and compare with the minimum possible.
restyleFix: Apply strategies F-24 to F-30.

title: Know the three cost components: cognitive, physical, time
rule: (1) Cognitive effort: mental processing needed to navigate; complex/unintuitive UI → high load; simple/intuitive → low. (2) Physical effort: number of clicks or keystrokes, amount of scrolling, etc. (3) Time effort: duration to reach the goal; slow loading, complex navigation, task complexity, lack of instructions raise it.
why: Gives audit lens for classifying friction.
doDont: n/a (conceptual; diagram only).
auditCheck: Classify each friction point under cognitive / physical / time.
restyleFix: Pick fix per component (simplify, shorten path, speed up/add instructions).

title: Minimise these measurable effort items
rule: Reduce the amount of: reading, scrolling, searching for useful information, understanding presented information, clicking/touching (without errors), typing, waiting for pages to load, and remembering information to complete a task. (Illustrated with a 15-icon grid of touch gestures — tap, swipe, drag, hold, multi-finger — from visual, decorative.)
why: These are the concrete sources of interaction cost.
doDont: n/a.
auditCheck: Checklist for a flow: long reading before action? long scroll to reach CTA? search needed? many taps/typing? loading waits? info that must be remembered across steps?
restyleFix: Cut copy, surface info, shorten forms, add autofill, speed up loads, keep context visible.

title: Cost is visible in the audit: don't expect zero, but target the biggest detours
rule: Zero interaction cost is the ultimate usability goal but is usually unrealistic; aim to reduce, not necessarily eliminate.
why: Feature-rich products inevitably require some interaction.
doDont: n/a.
auditCheck: Prioritise fixes on highest-frequency tasks with highest effort.
restyleFix: n/a (prioritisation guidance).

title: Keep related actions close (Fitts's Law)
rule: Closer and larger targets are faster to click. Position actions near the elements they relate to and give them a sufficient clickable area.
why: Fitts's Law — shorter distance and bigger target = less physical effort/time.
doDont: Do (Spotify, from visual): playback controls (shuffle, previous, play/pause, next, repeat + progress bar) in a persistent fixed bar at the bottom of the screen, highlighted in the screenshot, so users don't navigate to another screen/menu. Don't put the action far from its subject or behind a separate screen.
auditCheck: Distance between an action and the object it acts on; tiny hit areas (touch targets small); controls that require navigating away; CTA far from the related input.
restyleFix: Move controls adjacent to / persistently anchored with their target; enlarge hit areas.

title: Minimise choice (Hick's Law) and curate recommendations
rule: Decision time rises with the number and complexity of choices. Reduce options; highlight a smaller set of recommended/popular items.
why: Hick's Law — fewer choices → faster decisions.
doDont: Do (Uber Eats, from visual): curated horizontal carousels "Popular near you" and "New on Uber Eats" (4 cards each visible, "See all" links) instead of a list of hundreds of restaurants; filters (sort, price range, dietary) in a left sidebar. Don't dump hundreds of items/menu entries at once.
auditCheck: Count of equal-weight options presented at once (nav items, cards, menu items, filters); is there a recommended/popular/curated subset?
restyleFix: Group into curated sets, show top N with "See all", progressively disclose the rest.

title: Use working memory well: chunk information into ≈7 (±2) manageable groups
rule: People hold about seven items (give or take a couple) in working memory (George Miller). Organise information into meaningful, manageable chunks with clear headings.
why: Chunking reduces memory load.
doDont: Do (Airbnb listing, from visual): page split into separate boxed chunks — host summary ("Entire home hosted by… 10 guests · 4 bedrooms · 5 beds · 4 bathrooms"), highlights (Dedicated workspace, Unwind in the hot tub), description with "Show more", and "What this place offers" amenities grid with "Show all 21 amenities" — plus a sticky booking card (price £1,597/night, dates, guests, Reserve button, fee breakdown). Don't present a wall of text about the rental.
auditCheck: Long undivided text blocks; lists/menus/nav with >~7 ungrouped items; missing section headings.
restyleFix: Add headings, split into groups of ≲7, use "Show more"/"Show all N" to truncate long lists.

title: Reduce distractions
rule: Remove attention-diverting elements — animated banners, pop-ups, unnecessary visuals — from task and reading flows. Keep only content and essential navigation.
why: Distractions pull users away from completing tasks and raise interaction cost.
doDont: Do (Medium article page, from visual): clean minimal layout, one narrow centred column, big bold title, author line, small action row (clap/comment/save/play/share), hero image, body text; top bar only search/Write/notifications/avatar; no pop-ups/ads. Don't add banners, pop-ups, ads.
auditCheck: Auto-playing/animated banners, modals on load, ads, decorative imagery competing with main content in task screens.
restyleFix: Remove or defer pop-ups/banners; strip non-essential visuals and nav on focus pages.

title: Promote recognition over recall
rule: Let users recognise actions rather than recall from memory: use common symbols, icons, phrases and a logical layout; show remembered state such as progress.
why: Reduces mental effort, frustration and time.
doDont: Do (Disney+, from visual): a "Continue Watching" row at the top (highlighted yellow box) with progress bars under the thumbnails, remembering the episode/timestamp, followed by rows "What to Watch Tonight", "Recommended For You", "Action and Adventure". Don't make users remember which episode/timestamp they were at.
auditCheck: Does the UI make users remember info from earlier screens/sessions? Are icons unlabeled/unconventional? Is last-state/progress/recent items surfaced?
restyleFix: Add "recent/continue" shortcuts, visible state/progress, conventional icons with labels, recently used items.

title: Streamline tasks: remove or combine steps (autofill)
rule: Visualise the total number of steps in a process; remove or combine those that don't affect the outcome. Autofill address/credit-card details already entered.
why: Fewer steps lower physical interaction cost and raise efficiency.
doDont: Do (from visual): mobile checkout (Checkout → Add shipping address → Shipping address form → address field with typeahead suggestions e.g. "354 Oyster Point" → pick suggestion) — address autocomplete suggests full addresses; saved payment ("Pay with Visa •••• 4242") pre-filled. Don't make users retype saved data or go through avoidable steps.
auditCheck: Map steps in key flows (checkout, signup); count fields/screens; are there autofill (`autocomplete` attributes), address lookup, saved payment methods, combinable steps?
restyleFix: Merge/remove steps, enable autocomplete/address lookup, prefill known data.

title: Reduce repetition: automate or batch repetitive tasks
rule: Automate repetitive tasks or make them easier (bulk actions); reduces physical and cognitive costs.
why: Repetition multiplies effort.
doDont: Do (Google Sheets, from visual): fill-drag a formula/value across a selected range (cells A1:A17 selected) so one action applies to many cells. Don't force one-by-one edits.
auditCheck: Tasks users repeat per item (per row, per product) without bulk select/apply-to-all/duplicate/templates.
restyleFix: Add multi-select + bulk actions, copy/duplicate, templates, defaults, remember previous choices.

title: Don't hide options in dropdowns; show them (principle of visibility)
section: Interaction cost: worked example — product page (p.107-108)
rule: Choices hidden in dropdowns or nested menus may not be known to exist, causing missed opportunities and frustration. Show all options upfront (e.g. colour swatches) so users see choices immediately and can try several before deciding.
why: Reduces mental effort and clicks. Baseline cost: dropdown colour = 2 clicks + scroll, quantity dropdown = 2 more clicks + scroll, then mouse move + click on "Add to cart" → adding two red chairs costs five clicks, one scroll and a short mouse movement. Improved: changing colour = 1 click + short mouse move.
doDont: Bad ("Ergobliss chair", $199 USD): "Colour" dropdown showing "Green ⌄" and "Quantity" dropdown "1 ⌄", with "Add to cart" (red pill) placed far right. Good: three visible colour options (selected lime-green with ring, plus mustard and salmon swatches) — no dropdown.
auditCheck: `<select>`/dropdown used for a small set of options (≈ ≤5-6 options (inference)) that could be shown inline; count clicks to configure and buy.
restyleFix: Replace dropdown with inline swatches / segmented control / radio chips.

title: Replace text labels with visual samples (visual differentiation)
section: Interaction cost: worked example — product page (p.107-108)
rule: Show actual colour swatches instead of colour names as text; colour used as a visual cue is quickly understood.
why: Faster recognition than reading text.
doDont: Do circular colour swatches (selected one outlined with ring). Don't list "Green" as plain text in a dropdown.
auditCheck: Colour/material/pattern/size-image options presented as text only.
restyleFix: Use swatch chips (with selected state ring) for colour/visual attributes.

title: Use a quantity stepper (− / number / +) instead of a dropdown
section: Interaction cost: worked example — product page (p.107-108)
rule: Provide a selector where users click a plus sign or type the number directly, making small changes faster and easier. (Selector shown as bordered box: "−  1  +".)
why: Fewer clicks and no scroll vs dropdown.
doDont: Do stepper with minus, editable number and plus. Don't quantity dropdown "1 ⌄".
auditCheck: Quantity implemented as `<select>`; stepper missing direct numeric entry.
restyleFix: Replace with stepper (−/+ buttons + editable input).

title: Place the primary CTA next to the inputs it commits
section: Interaction cost: worked example — product page (p.107-108)
rule: Move the "Add to cart" button closer to the quantity selector to reduce interaction (mouse-travel) cost.
why: Fitts's Law — shorter distance; related actions close.
doDont: Good: "Add to cart" pill immediately right of the quantity stepper, below the colour swatches. Bad: "Add to cart" at far right edge, separated from the dropdowns.
auditCheck: Distance between configuration inputs and the submit CTA; CTA far-right/detached.
restyleFix: Re-lay out so the CTA sits adjacent to (right of or directly below) the final input.

title: Offer a primary "Buy now" (one-click order) button on product pages
rule: Reduce the steps between intent and purchase. Traditional shopping needs add to cart → checkout → enter shipping and payment details → confirm. One-Click Ordering lets users buy with a single click, skipping the checkout routine by using stored shipping and payment data. Add a primary "Buy now" button next to "Add to cart". Which of the two is the visually primary one depends on the business model and the UI's goals.
why: It sharply cuts the cognitive, physical and time effort (interaction cost) needed to place an order.
doDont: Do (shown): the Ergobliss chair product page ($199 USD) has a colour swatch selector (3 swatches, selected one ringed), a quantity stepper (− 1 +), and two pill buttons side by side. "Add to cart" is the outline/secondary style (pink outline, white fill). "Buy now" is the solid filled pink primary. No explicit bad example, but the implied bad case is a flow that forces cart → checkout → forms for every purchase.
auditCheck: On product or purchase screens, can a returning user with stored data complete the order in one click? Is there a one-step purchase CTA? Is the primary/secondary hierarchy between "Buy now" and "Add to cart" clear (filled vs outline) and a deliberate choice?
restyleFix: Add a filled primary "Buy now" button beside an outlined "Add to cart". Back it with saved address and payment. Keep one filled primary per decision area.

title: Don't hide content behind promotional banners that need a tap
rule: Don't put a big banner like "Discover 100+ recipes selected by our chefs" or "Discover 40+ foods that are good for your health" with an "Explore now" button between the user and the actual content. Show the content itself on the screen.
why: The banner is an extra step. Interaction cost is the cognitive, physical and time effort a user spends to reach their goal. Users want immediate value, and hiding content creates an unnecessary barrier between them and the value of the app. The cost looks trivial but adds up, especially for new users who are unsure about investing time.
auditCheck: Does a home or discovery screen use large banner/hero tiles whose only job is to say "explore X" and link elsewhere? Does each section show real items (cards/thumbnails with titles and metadata) at the point of entry? Count the taps from the screen to the first real content item (should be 0 (inference)).
restyleFix: Replace the banner with a horizontal row or grid of 3 actual item cards (image, title, key metadata such as duration). Add a small "View all" link on the right of the section header for the rest.

title: Show a curated, relevant list immediately (e.g. "Top 10 easy recommended recipes")
rule: On open, show a curated list (the PDF's example is "Top 10 easy recommended recipes") with no tap needed. Exposing content directly has three benefits: (1) Quick value, because the user instantly sees what the app offers and is more likely to engage; (2) Reduced friction, because fewer steps means a better experience, more retention and more interaction; (3) Relevancy, because you can showcase the most relevant or popular items so the user finds something of interest right away.
why: Instant value, lower friction and higher relevance improve retention and engagement.
doDont: Do: a ready list of specific, useful items on first view. Don't: generic "discover" teasers (see G-02).
auditCheck: Does the first viewport on a content app show specific, popular or relevant items rather than teasers? Are the items curated or ranked (e.g. "Top N")?
restyleFix: Replace teaser sections with a titled curated list ("Top 10 …") of actual items, ordered by popularity or relevance.

title: Design each input field for the type of data it collects
rule: Don't use a one-size-fits-all field. Shape each field (size, length, segmentation, typography) to match the information asked for.
why: It streamlines the interaction and removes unnecessary cognitive load, giving a smoother, more efficient experience.
doDont: See G-05 (verification code) and G-06 (card details) for the two examples.
auditCheck: Are all inputs in a form the same width and style regardless of the data they take? Is field width proportional to the expected value length?
restyleFix: Set field widths and segmentation by data type (see G-05, G-06).

title: Use separate large digit boxes for verification codes
rule: For a verification code, use individual big boxes, one per digit (the example has four boxes), with enlarged typography for the digits, instead of one long standard-text field.
why: It minimizes the chance of error by giving each digit a designated space, makes input quicker and less error-prone, and the larger digits are easy to tell apart, which helps users who struggle with small text.
auditCheck: Is a fixed-length code (OTP/PIN) entered into one single-line text field with default text size? Look for one `<input>` with no per-digit segmentation and font size equal to body size.
restyleFix: Replace it with N (e.g. 4) equal-sized boxes, one per digit. Use a large font size, auto-advance focus, and show a visible cursor/active state.

title: Match field length to expected data (short fields for CVC, expiry, zip) and pair them on a row
rule: Size each field by the type and amount of data it holds. A CVC is always 3 or 4 digits, so it gets a short field. Apply the same logic to expiry date (MM/YY) and zip code. Don't give every item its own full-width field.
why: Short fields remove ambiguity about what to type and make efficient use of space. The form then helps users enter data accurately and quickly, which benefits users and designers.
auditCheck: Are short-value fields (CVC 3-4 digits, expiry MM/YY, zip/postal code, quantity, age) rendered full width? Could two or more short fields share a row? A form with more than ~5 stacked full-width fields where some take ≤5 characters (inference) is a violation.
restyleFix: Set short fields to width proportional to content (about 1/3 to 1/2 of the row). Group related short fields side by side: Expiry+CVC, Country+Zip. Keep long data (card number, name) full width.

title: Don't use a "Confirm password" field
rule: Drop the outdated "Confirm password" field. Use a single password field. Its downsides: (1) Increased interaction cost, because each extra field is another thing to do. (2) Error-prone, because a mistake in confirmation often forces users to restart the whole process, which is frustrating and slow. (3) False sense of security, because users can mistype the same way twice, defeating the purpose.
why: The extra field adds effort and frustration, and doesn't deliver the safety it promises.
auditCheck: Does a sign-up or reset form contain a second password field (name/label/placeholder matching confirm/repeat/retype password, or two `type=password` inputs)?
restyleFix: Delete the confirm field. Add a show/hide toggle (G-08) and inline validation (G-09) to the single field.

title: Add a show/hide toggle to password fields
rule: Put a visibility toggle (eye icon) inside the password field so users can check what they typed without a second field. It keeps security while giving users control over visibility.
why: It replaces the confirm field and improves the experience of password fields.
doDont: Do (two states shown, both good): masked state shows dots with an "eye" icon on the right of the field. Revealed state shows the plain text "W$2SAmcxw" with an "eye-slash" icon. Both sit above the purple "Create account" button.
auditCheck: Does every password input have a toggle control (icon button, accessible label such as "Show password") inside or adjacent to the field? Is the icon state-reflective (eye vs eye-off)?
restyleFix: Add a trailing icon button inside the field that toggles `type=password` / `type=text`. Show eye when hidden and eye-slash when visible.

title: Use inline, real-time password validation
rule: Give feedback as the user types, not after submit. Keep it subtle but clear. Options: small checkmarks, colour changes, four bars (a strength meter), or brief messages below the password field.
why: Users can fix mistakes immediately, which reduces frustration and smooths account creation or password reset.
doDont: Do: under the password field (with eye toggle) is a 4-segment thin bar. The first segment is filled pink/red and the other three are light grey. Below it, the caption "**Weak** password strength" has the word "Weak" in the red colour and the rest in grey. The purple "Create account" button follows. Don't: only show an error after submit (implied).
auditCheck: Does password creation show rules/strength live while typing? Check for a strength meter, per-rule checkmarks or message. Does it appear only after submit?
restyleFix: Add a 4-bar strength indicator plus a one-line label below the field. Colour the filled bars and the label by strength (red for weak). Optionally add per-rule checkmarks.

title: Make the destructive confirm button red (not green)
rule: In a confirmation pop-up for a destructive or irreversible action (delete/remove), use red for the "Delete"/"Remove" button, following convention. Don't use green, which signals a positive or safe action and confuses users.
why: Red signals a destructive or irreversible action. Green misleads the user about the severity.
auditCheck: Is the button on a delete/remove/destroy dialog styled with a success/green or neutral primary colour instead of a danger colour (red)? Search for tokens like `btn-primary` or `bg-green-*` on destructive actions.
restyleFix: Use the danger/red token (e.g. `bg-red-*`/`--color-danger`) for the destructive confirm button. Keep green for positive actions.

title: Give users a way back: always include a Cancel option
rule: In destructive confirmations, include a visible Cancel option. Following conventions makes the interface more intuitive and reduces errors. A red button tells users it is an action to think twice about. Cancel acts as a safety net and reassures users they have control, reducing accidental errors.
why: A safety net that reassures users and reduces accidental errors.
doDont: Do (dark modal): title "Are you sure you want to delete your data?", sub-text "This action can't be undone.", a close "×" top right, a plain white-text "Cancel" on the left, and a pink/red "Delete" pill on the right. Don't: a modal with only "Delete" (see p.120 bad example).
auditCheck: Does a destructive confirm dialog have an explicit Cancel/dismiss button, rather than only the destructive action (a close "×" alone isn't enough)? Cancel should be styled as a secondary/text button.
restyleFix: Add a low-emphasis "Cancel" (text or ghost) button beside the red destructive button.

title: Place Cancel on the left and the destructive action on the right
rule: In confirmation pop-ups, put "Delete" on the right (signals moving forward, progressing the action) and "Cancel" on the left (signals a step back or retreat).
why: In left-to-right reading cultures, people scan interfaces the same way. The left Cancel is the first thing read, giving a quick exit before the more severe action on the right. This follows natural scanning patterns for a logical, efficient flow and reduces accidental deletions or cancellations.
auditCheck: In dialogs, is the destructive/confirm button left of the cancel button (in LTR locales)? In CSS: check the DOM/flex order of the footer buttons.
restyleFix: Reorder the footer to `[Cancel] [Delete]` (secondary first, primary last on the right). Note RTL locales would mirror this (inferred from the left-to-right rationale).

title: Avoid long, monolithic blocks of text
rule: Don't present product information as one dense paragraph. Attention is scarce. Users scan rather than read word-for-word (cited: Nielsen Norman Group research). Bite-sized information is easier to process.
why: A monolithic paragraph looks visually dull, makes reading laborious, overwhelms users and makes them bounce.
doDont: Don't: the UltraClean Vacuum Cleaner card has the product image on the left, and on the right the title and one very long paragraph (approx. 15+ lines) of small grey text. Only a few phrases are emphasized in darker/bold ("4.8-star customer rating", "HEPA filter", "cordless design", "conserving energy"). It is hard to scan.
auditCheck: Are there paragraphs longer than roughly 5-6 lines (inference) (the bad example runs about 15+ lines in a narrow column) in product/description areas? Does the description lack headings, lists or icons? Is bolding the only scan aid?
restyleFix: Break the paragraph into a short intro, a labelled list of key features, and a closing sentence (see G-14).

title: Divide content into logical sections with icons (checkmarks, stars)
rule: Split the same text into smaller, logically organized sections: a short intro, a "Key features:" list where each feature has a bold title, a one-line description and a tick icon, and a short closing paragraph. Use icons such as tick marks for key features and stars for reviews.
why: Icons are quicker to process than text and give an instant, clear point of focus. They break up the monotony, add a visual touch, and boost engagement.
doDont: Do: the same card now has the title "UltraClean Vacuum Cleaner", a star rating row (5 yellow stars, "**4.8** (3,2k reviews)"), a short intro paragraph, an underlined "Key features:" label, and four stacked features with green circular check icons, each with a dark title and a grey one-line description (Powerful Suction, HEPA Filter, Energy-Efficient, User-Friendly Controls), then a closing paragraph.
auditCheck: Do feature or benefit lists use plain sentences inside a paragraph instead of a list? Are ratings numeric only with no star icon? Are there headings or icons marking each point?
restyleFix: Convert features into a list with a leading icon (check) + bold title + one-line description. Add a stars + score + count row under the title (e.g. 4.8 (3,2k reviews)). Keep intro and outro short.

title: Lay features out in two columns
rule: Arrange the feature list in a two-column grid (2×2 in the example) instead of one long stack.
why: Visually it is balanced and symmetrical, uses screen real estate efficiently and looks less cluttered and more organized. For UX, users scan and compare features side-by-side with less scrolling. It also encourages chunking (grouping information into "chunks" that are easier to remember and understand).
doDont: Do: the same card with the features in a 2×2 grid.
